questions.a: Client abort, server abort of the vendor body, persist a cancelled partial, skip parse and tools. Write usage if you have it and show a stopped state in the UI.

questions.q: Why does aborting the body matter for the bill?
questions.a: Many providers stop generating (and stop charging unused tokens) when the client disconnects. If you keep reading, you pay for an answer the user already rejected.

questions.q: The stop handler sets `isLoading=false` and returns. What did they forget?
questions.a: Aborting the in-flight HTTP request and telling the server to abort the vendor stream. The model may still run and a tool may still fire.

questions.q: User hits stop, then types 'continue'. How do you implement that?
questions.a: New request id. Send the cancelled partial as assistant history plus a continue instruction. Do not try to resume the aborted socket.

questions.q: What finish reason do you store on a user stop?
questions.a: cancelled (or equivalent), never stop or success. That keeps evals and billing honest and prevents a parser from treating a partial as a record.

why-orchestration-libraries-exist.explain:
## What it is

An **orchestration library** (LangChain is the one this module names) sits between your application and one or more model-provider SDKs. It exists because the raw call is only the first five percent of a feature. You still need prompt templates, output parsers, tool wiring, retries, streaming adapters, and a way to swap `ChatOpenAI` for `ChatAnthropic` without rewriting the rest of the file. The library sells that glue.

What it abstracts: chat-model objects, message types, template variables, parsers that turn text or tool calls into Python objects, and a composition model (runnables / LCEL) so `prompt | model | parser` is a single object you can `invoke` or `stream`. What it does **not** abstract away: the HTTP call, the tokens you pay for, the schema you must still validate, or the fact that the model can be wrong.

LangChain is one such library, not a standard. LlamaIndex, vendor SDKs plus your own 80-line wrapper, and graph runners like LangGraph occupy the same niche with different tastes. The reason the category exists is repetition, not magic.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you will inherit a repo that imported LangChain because a tutorial did. Your job is to know what it is saving you from — and what it is hiding. Interviewers ask "why not just call OpenAI?" The junior answer is "LangChain is industry standard". The senior answer is "it is glue for templates, parsers, and provider adapters; I still own retries, logs, and schemas; I can do the same with a thin wrapper if the glue is all I needed".

This question also filters cargo-cult. If you cannot name the raw request the library will make, you do not understand your production path.

## How it works + one small example

Draw two columns on the whiteboard.

Raw SDK: build messages by hand, call `client.chat.completions.create`, `json.loads` the content, retry yourself, swap providers by rewriting the call.

LangChain: `ChatPromptTemplate` → `ChatOpenAI` → `JsonOutputParser`, `.with_structured_output`, `.bind_tools`. The invoke is one line. The HTTP call is still a chat completion with those messages.

Example. A classifier you wrote in 40 lines of raw SDK. The LangChain version is 25 lines and can change the model class in one import. The rendered prompt, the token bill, and the need to validate the parsed object did not go away. You print those, not the chain name, when it misbehaves.

Choose the library when you will actually use composition, tools, and provider ports. Choose the raw SDK when the feature is one call and you want a short stack trace.

## Failure modes

1. **Library as the product.** The domain model is a `Chain`. You cannot test or replace the vendor without dragging the framework.

2. **Not knowing the underlying call.** A timeout or a 400 appears as a LangChain error. You cannot read the request that failed.

3. **Glue you do not use.** You imported the universe for a single `invoke`. Dependency and upgrade cost with no composition benefit.

4. **Assuming abstraction removes validation.** The parser returned a dict. The dict is still untrusted.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask what raw HTTP call the chain will make and which glue they are actually using. If they cannot name the request, they do not understand the layer. If the feature is one call and they imported the universe, ask them to justify the dependency.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Orchestration libraries are glue: templates, parsers, provider adapters, and a composition model. They are not the LLM. I use them when that glue pays for itself, and I still own the rendered prompt, the schema, and the logs.
keyPoints: Libraries exist to reuse templates, parsers, tools, and provider adapters.
LangChain is glue over HTTP calls, not a different model.
You still own retries, logging, schemas, and the rendered prompt.
The category is bigger than one brand: wrappers and graph runners count.
Pick the library when you will use composition, not because a tutorial did.
If you cannot name the underlying request, you cannot debug production.

questions.q: What does an orchestration library abstract, and what does it not?
questions.a: It abstracts templates, message types, parsers, provider adapters, and composition. It does not abstract the HTTP call, the token bill, correctness, or the need to validate output.

questions.q: A candidate says they used LangChain because it is the industry standard. What is the stronger reason?
questions.a: They needed reuse: prompt templates, a parser, tools, or a provider port. Standard is not a reason. A thin raw-SDK wrapper is enough for one call.

questions.q: A LangChain chain throws a wrapped 400. What do you inspect first?
questions.a: The rendered messages and the underlying provider request, not the chain class name. Confirm model id, token length, and schema. The library is a wrapper around that call.

questions.q: When would you refuse LangChain for a new feature?
questions.a: A single structured call with no tools and no provider swap in sight. A 40-line SDK wrapper will be easier to debug and to pin. Add a library when composition actually appears.

questions.q: Why is 'LangChain is the model' a broken mental picture?
questions.a: The model is the vendor endpoint (or the weights). LangChain is an orchestration layer that builds the request and parses the response. Quality, price, and outages live at the model.

models-templates-output-parsers.explain:
## What it is

LangChain's useful core is three objects you should be able to name. A **chat model** is a callable wrapper around a provider (messages in, a message or a parsed object out), with config for temperature, tools, and streaming. A **prompt template** is a string or chat message list with variables (`{ticket}`, `{policy}`) that renders to concrete messages. An **output parser** turns the model's text or tool payload into a typed object — or fails.

Together they are `prompt | model | parser`. Streaming is a method on the same runnable (`stream` / `astream`), not a different pipeline. Model configuration (temperature, `max_tokens`, model id) lives on the model object so the template stays reusable.

These objects do not replace your schema. A parser that "usually works" is not validation. Treat parser success as syntactic, then apply your own checks.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the vocabulary of a LangChain codebase. If you cannot point at the template, the model, and the parser, you will edit the wrong file when the label set changes. Interviewers ask you to walk `prompt | model | parser` and say where you would log. The senior answer: log the **rendered** prompt and the **parsed** object, plus usage from the model.

They also want you to know that swapping the model object is how you change providers, and swapping the parser is how you change the contract — not by stuffing "please return JSON" into the template.

## How it works + one small example

A ticket classifier:

- Template: system rules + `{ticket}` last.
- Model: `ChatOpenAI(model=..., temperature=0)` with structured output or a tool.
- Parser: Pydantic / JSON schema for `{label, reason}`.

`chain = template | model | parser`. `chain.invoke({"ticket": text})` returns a dict. `chain.stream(...)` yields chunks; you still parse at the end unless you use a streaming parser.

When it fails, print `template.format(...)` (or the messages the model received) and the raw message **before** the parser. A parser error is often a truncated or refused completion, not a "LangChain bug".

## Failure modes

1. **Business rules in the template only.** The parser accepts any string. You wanted an enum. Put the enum in the schema.

2. **Logging the chain name.** `classifier_v3` tells you nothing. Log rendered messages and the parsed object.

3. **A new model object per request, with a clock in the template.** You bust caches and you cannot A/B the template separately.

4. **Parser that swallows errors.** It returns `{}` on failure. Downstream writes empty rows. Fail loud, then repair.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to point at the template, the model config, and the parser in the diff. Ask where they log the rendered messages. If the only log is the chain class name, the review fails.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Core objects: chat model, prompt template, output parser.
- Composition is prompt | model | parser, with stream as a method.
- Templates hold variables; models hold temperature, tools, and ids.
- Parser success is syntactic; you still validate business rules.
- Debug with the rendered messages and the raw model output.
- Do not hide failures inside a parser that returns empty dicts.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A parser raises on 10% of turns. Where do you look first? The raw model message and finish reason, then the rendered prompt. Truncation, a refusal, or a schema the model missed will show there. The chain name will not. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Where should allowed labels live — template, model, or parser/schema? In the schema (enum) that the parser and, ideally, structured-output decoding enforce. The template may mention them; the contract is the schema. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What are the three core LangChain objects in a simple pipeline? A prompt template (variables → messages), a chat model (provider call, config, streaming), and an output parser (text or tool payload → a typed object). They compose as prompt | model | parser. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I build `prompt | model | parser`: the template owns variables, the model owns provider config and streaming, the parser owns shape. I log the rendered prompt and the parsed object, and I still validate.

working-across-providers.explain:
## What it is

LangChain's pitch includes **one interface, many providers**. You construct `ChatOpenAI`, `ChatAnthropic`, or `ChatGoogleGenerativeAI` with the same message types and, often, the same `invoke` / `stream` / `bind_tools` methods. That is real reuse. It is not sameness underneath. Each class still makes that vendor's HTTP call, with that vendor's role names, token limits, tool-call shapes, and safety flags.

Working across providers means you can swap the class for a prototype, and it means you **still read the request** that class will send. System prompts may need to move from a message to a top-level parameter. Tool schemas may need a slightly different JSON Schema subset. Structured output may be native on one vendor and a tool hack on another.

The library reduces rewriting. It does not give you one behaviour.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a PM will ask "can we flip to Vendor B this week?". If you hid the provider behind a port, yes for the happy path. If you depended on a vendor-specific finish reason or a 200k context, no. Interviewers want both sentences: the adapter makes the swap cheap, and you still verify tools, schemas, and limits on the new endpoint.

They will also ask whether LangChain "locks you in". The honest answer: it can, if your domain imports LangChain types everywhere. Keep your own message and schema types at the boundary.

## How it works + one small example

Put a factory behind your port:

`def chat_model(name: str) -> BaseChatModel` that returns the right class from env. Application code talks to the port. The first time you add Anthropic next to OpenAI, you run the **same eval set** and you print one raw request per vendor.

Example. OpenAI structured output uses a response format. Anthropic may use a tool or a native schema flag depending on the month. Your parser still validates the same Pydantic model. If Vendor B cannot enumerate your 40 labels natively, you keep the enum in local validation and a repair loop. The factory did not remove that work; it removed the need to rewrite the template.

Never switch providers in production on a Friday without an eval. The interface matching is necessary, not sufficient.

## Failure modes

1. **Assuming identical behaviour.** Temperature, refusals, and tool-call batching differ. Users see it.

2. **Leaking vendor types into the domain.** `AIMessage` everywhere. A later swap rewrites the app, not just the factory.

3. **Skipping the raw request.** You cannot explain a 400 that only happens on Vendor B.

4. **Context-window surprise.** Vendor A accepted 20k tokens of history; Vendor B 400s. Your windowing policy is part of the port.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for the eval result on the second provider and one raw request dump. An unused ChatX import is not portability. Ask which domain types still mention the first vendor.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- One interface, many providers — reuse of invoke, stream, and tools.
- Underneath, each class still makes a vendor-specific HTTP call.
- Re-run evals and print a raw request when you add a provider.
- Keep application types off LangChain and vendor classes.
- Window size, tool shape, and structured-output support still differ.
- A factory is a port; it is not a guarantee of identical behaviour.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You flipped ChatOpenAI to ChatAnthropic and 8% of tool calls broke. What do you do first? Print the raw request and the tool-schema each class sent. Confirm role placement, JSON Schema subset, and how parallel calls are expressed. Then fix the adapter or the schema, not the prompt copy first. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you keep a provider swap from rewriting the app? A factory behind a port, and your own message/schema types at the boundary. Application code does not import ChatOpenAI or AIMessage. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What do you gain, and what do you not, by using LangChain across providers? You gain a shared invoke/stream/tools surface and cheaper template reuse. You do not gain identical behaviour, limits, or error shapes. Each class still calls its vendor. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

LangChain lets me swap a chat-model class, but each class still makes that vendor's call. I keep my own types at the boundary, I re-run evals on a swap, and I read one raw request per provider.

questions.a: Print the raw request and the tool-schema each class sent. Confirm role placement, JSON Schema subset, and how parallel calls are expressed. Then fix the adapter or the schema, not the prompt copy first.

questions.q: How do you keep a provider swap from rewriting the app?
questions.a: A factory behind a port, and your own message/schema types at the boundary. Application code does not import ChatOpenAI or AIMessage.

questions.q: What must you run before promoting a second provider?
questions.a: The same eval set, plus a check of context limits, structured-output support, and one logged raw request. Interface compatibility is not quality compatibility.

questions.q: Why might a system prompt need to move when you change vendors?
questions.a: Some APIs take system as a top-level field, others as a message role. The adapter usually handles this, but custom message assembly can bypass it and 400.

composing-pipelines-with-runnables.explain:
## What it is

LangChain's composition model is the **runnable**: an object with `invoke`, `stream`, `batch`, and often `ainvoke`. Prompts, models, parsers, and functions can all be runnables. The pipe operator builds a **runnable sequence**. Other combinators fan out, branch, or map over lists. The point is that a pipeline is a value you can pass, test, and wrap with callbacks — not a pile of nested function calls you cannot see.

A simple pipeline is `prompt | model | parser`. A slightly richer one is a router that picks one of two chains, or a fan-out that runs two retrieves and merges. You should be able to build the simple one and explain the richer ones without claiming you need an agent.

Runnables do not remove control flow from your brain. An `if` you can read in your handler is still better than a clever combinator you cannot step through.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, LCEL (this composition style) is how a lot of sample code is written. You will have to read it. Interviewers may ask you to compose a classifier or a retrieve-then-generate on a whiteboard using pipes. They want to see a clear sequence and a place for logging, not a spaghetti of lambdas.

They also want the sentence that you built the same flow by hand first, so you know what the pipe is hiding. That is the next-but-one note; plant it here.

## How it works + one small example

Start with the hand-written function: render prompt, call model, parse, return. Then replace it with `chain = prompt | model | parser` and assert the same tests.

Example. Input `{ticket}`. Prompt renders system + ticket. Model returns a message. Parser yields `{label, reason}`. You add a callback or a wrapper that logs rendered messages and usage. For a two-step flow (extract entities, then classify), compose two sequences and call them in your own function first. Only then try a pipe of pipes.

`batch` is for many independent inputs with bounded concurrency — see M2.8. Do not `batch` a user-facing turn that has a 20s timeout just because the method exists.

## Failure modes

1. **Pipes you cannot debug.** A five-stage LCEL graph with anonymous lambdas. You cannot print the middle. Prefer named runnables or a plain function.

2. **Composition as a goal.** The feature needed one `if`. You built a router runnable. The next hire cannot find the branch.

3. **Forgetting the input schema.** The pipe expects a dict with `ticket`; you passed a string. The error is a missing key deep in the stack.

4. **Streaming the whole pipe blindly.** A parser in the middle breaks the stream. Stream the model; parse at the end.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to walk the pipe on a whiteboard and to name each stage. If a documented if was replaced by an anonymous router, ask them to put the if back. Ask how they stream without parsing every delta.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Runnables expose invoke, stream, and batch on prompts, models, and parsers.
- prompt | model | parser is the default sequence.
- Name stages so you can log the middle of the pipe.
- A readable if in your handler beats a clever combinator.
- Build the flow by hand first, then reproduce it with pipes.
- Stream the model; parse at the end of the sequence.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A piped chain fails with a missing-key error. How do you debug? Print the input dict and the output of each named stage. The pipe expects specific keys (for example ticket). Anonymous lambdas hide which stage broke. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When do you keep control flow in your own function instead of LCEL? When the branch is a documented if/else, a retry, or a join that must handle a failed arm. Readable application code is easier to test than a clever combinator. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What methods does a LangChain runnable typically expose? invoke (one input), stream (incremental output), batch (many inputs), and async variants. Prompts, models, parsers, and functions can all be runnables. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A runnable is a composable invoke/stream/batch object. I pipe prompt, model, and parser when the flow is a sequence, I name the stages, and I still write a plain function when the control flow is an if.

A readable if in your handler beats a clever combinator.

Stream the model; parse at the end of the sequence.

questions.a: So you know the control flow, the exact messages, and the failure paths. The pipe should reproduce a flow you already understand, not invent one you cannot step through.

raw-sdk-vs-langchain.explain:
## What it is

You should be able to write the **same feature twice**: once with the provider SDK, once with LangChain. The comparison is the point of this topic. Raw SDK: explicit messages, explicit HTTP options, explicit parse, a stack trace that is eight frames long. LangChain: templates, a model class, a parser, a shorter happy path, a stack trace that is eighty frames long when it fails.

Convenience is real: tools, structured output, and provider ports arrive faster. Abstraction overhead is also real: versions move, imports are heavy, errors wrap the useful one, and you can lose the rendered prompt if you never print it. Neither column wins for every feature.

The interview move is to pick a concrete task (classifier, one tool, a two-step extract-then-summarise) and say which lines disappear in each version — and which lines **must not** disappear (timeout, usage log, validation).

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, teams pick LangChain by default and then cannot upgrade it, or they ban it and re-implement templates badly. The grown-up process is to implement the first version raw so you know the call, then adopt the library where the glue is repetitive. Interviewers will ask you to compare. A brand-loyal answer ("we only use X") scores worse than a comparison on debug time, dependency cost, and speed of the first feature.

## How it works + one small example

Take a structured classifier.

Raw: 30–50 lines. Env key, messages list, `response_format` or a tool, `json.loads`, Pydantic validate, log usage, timeout. You can read it top to bottom.

LangChain: 20–30 lines. Template, `with_structured_output`, invoke. You still add timeout, usage callback, and a local validate. If you skip those, the library version is shorter and worse.

Time both to a passing test. Time both to a diagnosed 400. Often the raw version loses the first race and wins the second. That is the overhead you are buying.

When the feature grows a second provider and three tools, the library column usually wins the first race by more. Re-run the comparison; do not freeze a decision from week one.

## Failure modes

1. **Library without the production lines.** No timeout, no usage, no validate. Shorter and unsafe.

2. **Raw SDK copy-pasted six times.** You refused the library and then forked your own worse one.

3. **Comparing line counts only.** Debug time and upgrade risk do not appear in `wc -l`.

4. **Never printing the raw equivalent.** You cannot explain the LangChain path in an interview or an incident.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see the production lines — timeout, usage, validate — in the LangChain version. A shorter sample that dropped those lines is worse than the raw SDK. Ask how long a 400 takes to diagnose.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Implement once raw and once with LangChain so the comparison is concrete.
- Convenience: templates, tools, structured output, provider ports.
- Overhead: deep stacks, wrapping errors, dependency and upgrade cost.
- Timeout, usage, and validation must exist in both versions.
- Re-evaluate when tools and providers multiply; do not freeze week-one taste.
- Line count is a weak metric; diagnosis time is a better one.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A LangChain 400 has an 80-frame stack and a wrapped error. What do you do? Unwrap until you see the provider body, then print the rendered messages. Compare to the raw-SDK request you should be able to write. Fix that request, not the pipe syntax. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When does the raw SDK usually win? One or two calls, one provider, a team that wants short stack traces. When you would use ten percent of the library and pay for one hundred percent of the upgrades. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Name two things LangChain usually makes shorter and two it does not remove. Shorter: prompt templates, provider ports, tool wiring, structured-output helpers. Not removed: timeouts, usage logging, schema validation, and reading the rendered prompt when it fails. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I can write the feature on the raw SDK and on LangChain. The library buys templates, parsers, and ports. I still add timeout, usage, and validation, and I pick the stack by debug time and repetition, not by brand.

Convenience: templates, tools, structured output, provider ports.
Overhead: deep stacks, wrapping errors, dependency and upgrade cost.
Timeout, usage, and validation must exist in both versions.
Re-evaluate when tools and providers multiply; do not freeze week-one taste.
Line count is a weak metric; diagnosis time is a better one.

questions.a: Shorter: prompt templates, provider ports, tool wiring, structured-output helpers. Not removed: timeouts, usage logging, schema validation, and reading the rendered prompt when it fails.

questions.a: One or two calls, one provider, a team that wants short stack traces. When you would use ten percent of the library and pay for one hundred percent of the upgrades.

questions.a: Several tools, a provider port you will actually swap, and repeated template-plus-parser composition. The glue is then less code than the forks you would write.

questions.a: Timeout, request id, usage/finish-reason logging, local validation, and a way to print the rendered prompt. The sample's invoke line is the happy path only.

langchain-is-a-layer-not-the-model.explain:
## What it is

Keep this sentence in your head: **LangChain is an orchestration layer, not the LLM**. The model is the thing that predicts tokens — a vendor endpoint or a local server. LangChain builds the request, routes it, and parses the response. Quality, price, context limits, and outages belong to the model (and the vendor). Templates, parsers, and pipes belong to the layer.

People blur this because the import is `ChatOpenAI` and the demo looks like "the chain answered". In production the chain did not answer. The model did. The chain assembled the messages. If you swap the model class and quality drops, you changed the model. If you swap the parser and a field goes missing, you changed the layer.

This mental model also tells you what to pin and what to eval. Pin model ids and prompt versions. Pin library versions so upgrades are chosen. Do not pin "LangChain" as if it were a brain.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, incident channels fill with "LangChain is down" when OpenAI is 503, and "the model is dumb" when your parser stripped a field. Interviewers listen for the split. Candidates who say "we use LangChain" as an architecture have not made it. Candidates who say "LangChain calls Vendor X with this schema; the model is Y" have.

Hiring managers also use this to test whether you can leave the library. If the layer is not the model, you can replace the layer.

## How it works + one small example

In every design doc, write two lines:

- Model: `vendor / id / snapshot`, context limit, price.
- Layer: LangChain (or raw SDK / LangGraph / custom), version, what it owns (templates, tools, retries if any).

Example. p95 latency jumped. You check the vendor status and your TTFT. The layer did not get slower; prefill did. Second example: a field vanished after an upgrade. The model still emitted it; a parser change dropped unknowns. You rolled back the layer, not the model.

When someone asks "can we switch off LangChain?", you answer from the port: if your domain talks to a `complete(messages) -> Result` interface, yes. If your domain is 40 imports of LCEL, no — you coupled to the layer.

## Failure modes

1. **Incidents filed against the wrong owner.** You page the library authors for a vendor outage.

2. **Evals that name only the chain.** You cannot tell a model regression from a parser regression.

3. **Treating the layer as lock-in you cannot leave.** That is a boundary problem you created.

4. **Upgrading the library and the model on the same day.** You cannot attribute the quality drop.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask who they would page if p95 jumped versus if a field vanished after a library upgrade. If both answers are LangChain, they have not split the layer from the model. Ask where the port lives.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- The model predicts tokens; LangChain assembles and parses the call.
- Quality, price, and vendor outages belong to the model.
- Templates, parsers, and pipes belong to the layer.
- Pin model ids and library versions separately.
- Incidents and evals must say which side moved.
- A port makes the layer replaceable; importing LCEL everywhere does not.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Latency jumps and someone says 'LangChain is slow'. How do you split the blame? Measure TTFT and vendor status first (model/prefill/network). Then check whether the layer added retries or extra calls. Do not page the library for a 503 at the vendor. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you keep the option to delete LangChain later? Put a port in front (`complete(messages) -> Result`) and keep domain types off LangChain classes. The layer becomes a plugin, not the application. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: In one sentence, what is LangChain relative to the LLM? An orchestration layer that builds requests and parses responses. The LLM is the vendor endpoint or local server that generates tokens. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

LangChain is a layer that builds and parses calls. The model is the endpoint that predicts tokens. I pin and eval them separately, I page the owner of the failure, and I keep a port so the layer is replaceable.

Templates, parsers, and pipes belong to the layer.

A port makes the layer replaceable; importing LCEL everywhere does not.

vendor-lock-in-vs-raw-sdk.explain:
## What it is

"Vendor lock-in" in this module is two different bindings. **Provider lock-in** is when your code, prompts, and schemas only work on one vendor's API. **Framework lock-in** is when your domain only works through LangChain types. A raw SDK can lock you to a vendor. A framework can lock you to itself while *claiming* to free you from vendors. You still own **retries, logging, and schemas** in both cases. Those are the pieces that make a swap possible.

Hiding a provider behind `ChatX` does not hide the contract you actually depend on: context length, tool-call shape, structured-output flags, safety behaviour. If those leak into your features, you are locked no matter how pretty the adapter is.

The antidote is boring: your own result type, your own schema, your own usage row, your own retry map. The SDK or the framework becomes a driver.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, leadership will ask "are we locked into OpenAI?" after a price change, and "are we locked into LangChain?" after a painful upgrade. Interviewers ask the same with different words. The senior answer names both locks and the three things you refuse to outsource: retries, logs, schemas. "We use LangChain so we are portable" without those three is a slogan.

This is also how you keep a take-home honest. If the rubric says "any provider", your schema and logs should not mention one vendor.

## How it works + one small example

Write a port:

```
class LlmPort:
    def complete(self, messages, schema, tools, timeout) -> Result
```

`Result` has `text | tool_calls`, `usage`, `finish`, `served_model`, `request_id`. Retries live in a wrapper around the port. Schemas are Pydantic / JSON Schema you own. LangChain or the OpenAI SDK implements the port.

Example. You move from OpenAI to Anthropic. You change the driver. The retry map still says 429/503 retry, 401 fail. The usage row still has prompt/completion/cache. The schema still rejects a missing `label`. If any of those lived only inside a vendor helper, the move would have rewritten the app.

Do a fire-drill once: run the eval suite on a second driver for a weekend. That is the only proof of portability.

## Failure modes

1. **Portability as an import.** You imported a second chat model class and declared victory. Evals were never run.

2. **Retries only inside the framework defaults.** You cannot explain or change them. A vendor swap changes retry behaviour silently.

3. **Schemas as prompt text.** "Please return JSON" in a vendor-specific tool wrapper. Local validation never existed.

4. **Logs that only a vendor dashboard can read.** You cannot compare two providers on your own grain.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask where retries, logs, and schemas live. If any of the three exist only as framework defaults, the port is fake. Ask when they last ran the eval suite on a second driver.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Provider lock and framework lock are different bindings.
- You still own retries, logs, and schemas on any stack.
- A port with your Result type makes either driver replaceable.
- Context limits and tool shapes can lock you even behind an adapter.
- Portability is an eval on a second driver, not a second import.
- Do not leave retry policy only in framework defaults.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A lead says you are portable because ChatAnthropic is one import away. What is missing? A real second driver behind a port, your own Result type, and an eval run on that driver. An unused import does not prove limits, tools, or quality match. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How can a raw SDK be less locking than a framework? If you wrapped the SDK in a small port, the domain never saw vendor types. A framework used everywhere can be the harder lock even while it offers more vendors. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What three things should you own even if a framework hides the vendor? Retry policy (what is retried, timeouts, caps), usage/finish-reason logging, and schemas with local validation. Those survive a vendor or library swap. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Frameworks hide providers; I still own retries, logging, and schemas. Those three are the port. Vendor lock and framework lock are both real, and an unused second import is not portability.

questions.a: In your wrapper around the port, documented as 429/503 retry and 400/401 fail (unless you have a reason). Not only as a hidden framework default.

debugging-through-a-runnable.explain:
## What it is

A runnable that failed is not debugged by staring at its class name. You need the **rendered prompt** (the exact messages the model received) and the **raw model output** before the parser, plus usage and finish reason. LangChain can hide all three behind a pipe. Your job is to make them printable on every environment you will actually use — local, staging, a single production request id.

Callbacks, `verbose`, tracing products (LangSmith and others), or a thin wrapper that logs at each named stage all work. What does not work is adding `print(chain)` or reading only the exception type. The useful artefacts are bytes the vendor saw and bytes it returned.

Once you have those, debugging a runnable is debugging a raw call. That is the point of the previous notes.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, LCEL failures are a rite of passage: a missing key, a parser error, a silent empty dict. The teams that survive have a "dump the render" habit. Interviewers will say "the chain returned the wrong label" and watch whether you ask for the rendered prompt. If you ask for the chain version or the model name only, you are guessing.

This is also how you keep a framework honest. If you cannot print the render, you do not control the layer.

## How it works + one small example

Name every stage. Wrap invoke:

1. Log input dict (redacted).
2. Log `prompt.format_messages(...)` or equivalent.
3. Log raw `AIMessage` / tool calls / finish / usage.
4. Log parsed object or the parser exception.

Example. Label is `other` for a clear billing ticket. The render shows the ticket variable was empty because the handler passed `text` not `ticket`. The model classified an empty string. The parser was fine. Without the render you would have "tuned the prompt" for a week.

In production, gate the full render behind a policy (PII). Always keep usage, finish reason, and a hash of the prompt. For a single incident, an admin flag should dump the render for that request id.

## Failure modes

1. **Class-name debugging.** `StrOutputParser` failed. That is a category, not a cause.

2. **Verbose everywhere, readable nowhere.** You logged megabytes and cannot find the messages. Prefer one structured dump per stage.

3. **No render in staging.** You only have it locally. The bug is data-dependent and staging is where the data lives.

4. **Parser swallows, so you never dump.** Empty dict, HTTP 200, wrong row. Fail loud.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to produce the rendered prompt for a failing request id. If they cannot, the pipeline is not debuggable. Ask how PII is gated on that dump.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- The artefacts are the rendered messages and the raw model output.
- Name runnable stages so the middle of the pipe is printable.
- Usage and finish reason belong next to the raw output.
- A missing template key looks like a 'model' bug until you print the render.
- Gate full prompts for PII; always keep usage and a prompt hash.
- Parser errors should be loud so a dump exists.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The model 'returns other' for every ticket. The parser is happy. What might the render show? An empty or wrong template variable (handler passed text instead of ticket), or a truncated ticket. You would have tuned the wording in vain without the render. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you get a dump in production without logging every user's prompt? Always log usage, finish reason, model, and a prompt hash. Dump the full render for a single request id behind an admin/PII policy when you are investigating. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What two artefacts do you print first when a LangChain pipeline is wrong? The rendered messages the model actually received, and the raw model output (plus finish reason) before the parser. The chain class name is not an artefact. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I debug a runnable by printing the rendered prompt and the raw model output, not the chain name. Named stages, a dump per request id, and the same inspector I use on the raw SDK.

questions.a: Always log usage, finish reason, model, and a prompt hash. Dump the full render for a single request id behind an admin/PII policy when you are investigating.

questions.q: Why name stages in a pipe instead of using anonymous lambdas?
questions.a: So you can log or breakpoint the middle. Anonymous functions turn a parser error into an unreadable stack with no render.

questions.q: A teammate turns on verbose=True and still cannot find the messages. What do you change?
questions.a: Structured per-stage logs (or a tracer) that emit rendered messages and raw output as fields, not a firehose of internals. Verbose is not a dump you can query.

schema-constrained-generation.explain:
## What it is

**Schema-constrained generation** means the model is not free to emit any text you later hope is JSON. The provider (or a grammar / JSON-schema decoder) **restricts the next tokens** so the completion is valid against a schema: required keys, types, enums, nested objects. This is different from writing "please return JSON" in the prompt. Prompting is a request. A constraint is a fence.

Vendors expose this as structured outputs, response formats, tool-call arguments with a schema, or grammar decoding. Frameworks wrap those flags. The point is the same: you want a parseable object with a known shape, not a chatty paragraph that sometimes contains braces.

Constraints buy **syntax**. They do not buy truth. A perfectly valid `{ "label": "billing" }` can still be the wrong label. The next notes in this module are about validation and repair; this one is about not starting from a string you cannot parse.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the first integration with a database or a UI state machine dies on unparseable text. Teams waste a week on prompt adjectives before they turn on the schema flag. Interviewers will ask "how do you get JSON out of a model?". The junior answer is the please-return-JSON line. The senior answer is constrained decoding (or a tool schema), then local validation, then a repair loop. They may also ask why you still validate: because a valid object can be a lie.

This is one of the highest-leverage Level 2 skills. Take-homes that regex JSON out of markdown look junior.

## How it works + one small example

Pick the native flag for your vendor. Define a schema (JSON Schema or a Pydantic / zod model). Send it on the call. Parse with your local model, not with a regex.

Example. Labels `billing | bug | how-to | other`. Without a constraint, the model returns `Label: Billing.` or a fenced markdown block. With a constraint, you get `{"label":"billing","reason":"..."}` or a tool-call payload that already matches. You still run `Schema.parse(...)` locally because you do not trust the vendor's decoder with your process memory.

If the vendor cannot constrain (older models, some hosts), you fall back to a tool schema or a grammar, and you keep the repair loop. You do not pretend a prompt is a decoder.

## Failure modes

1. **Prompt-only JSON.** It works in the demo. It breaks in production on long answers and refusals.

2. **Trusting the constraint as truth.** Valid JSON, wrong refund. Validation of meaning is separate.

3. **Regex "just in case".** You extract the first `{...}` from a paragraph and silently accept a truncated object.

4. **Schema so loose it is a string.** `{ "data": string }` with JSON inside the string. You built a prompt again.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which native flag the call sets and what the parse-fail rate is. If the answer is we asked it to return JSON, reject the PR. Ask where local validation still runs after the constraint.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Constrained decoding fences tokens to a schema; a prompt only asks.
- Use the vendor's structured-output or tool-schema flag first.
- Syntax is not truth: valid JSON can still be the wrong answer.
- Parse with your local schema library, not a regex on markdown.
- A schema that is one free-form string is not a constraint.
- If the vendor cannot constrain, keep a repair loop — do not hope.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Your parser fails on markdown-fenced JSON about 15% of the time. First fix? Turn on native structured output or a tool schema so the model cannot emit the fence. Keep local parse as a check. Do not start with a stronger regex. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why do you still run Pydantic/zod after a constrained call succeeds? Vendor decoders can change, optional fields can be missing, and you want one schema in your process. Also, constraint does not check business meaning. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is the difference between 'please return JSON' and schema-constrained generation? The first is a prompt request the model can ignore. The second restricts tokens (or tool arguments) so the completion must match a schema. One is hope; the other is a fence. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I get structured output from a schema constraint, not from 'please return JSON'. That buys syntax. I still validate locally because a valid object can be semantically wrong.

Use the vendor's structured-output or tool-schema flag first.
Syntax is not truth: valid JSON can still be the wrong answer.
Parse with your local schema library, not a regex on markdown.
A schema that is one free-form string is not a constraint.
If the vendor cannot constrain, keep a repair loop — do not hope.

questions.a: The first is a prompt request the model can ignore. The second restricts tokens (or tool arguments) so the completion must match a schema. One is hope; the other is a fence.

questions.q: When is a schema too weak to count as a constraint?
questions.a: When the only field is a free-form string (or a blob) that you will parse again. Tight enums, required keys, and typed lists are the point.

questions.a: No. It means the shape parsed. Semantic correctness — the right label, the real order id — is a separate check against your data or a judge.

defining-schemas.explain:
## What it is

A useful schema is a **contract**, not a sketch. You define it in JSON Schema or a typed model (Pydantic, zod, dataclasses). You mark **required** vs **optional** on purpose. You use **enums** for closed sets, **lists** for repeated items, and **nested objects** for records that have parts (an address, a citation). You give fields names a stranger could implement, and you describe them in the schema text the model will see.

Loose schemas produce loose objects. `{"notes": string}` invites a paragraph. `{"label": enum, "reason": string, "order_id": string | null}` can be checked, stored, and tested. Optional is not "whatever". Optional means "absent is legal; if present, this type". Required means "reject or repair if missing".

The same schema should drive the vendor constraint, the local validator, and the TypeScript/Python type your app uses. Three copies that drift are how you ship `reason` to one side and `rationale` to the other.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, schema design is API design. Interviewers will put a sloppy `{data: any}` on the board and ask you to tighten it. They want enums, required keys, a null vs missing story, and nested objects instead of encoded strings. They also want you to say the schema is shared — generated or imported — not pasted twice.

A take-home that uses a typed model scores higher than one that `json.loads` into an untyped dict and indexes keys with hope.

## How it works + one small example

Write the object you want to store, then the schema.

Example. Ticket classifier:

```
label: enum[billing, bug, how-to, other]   # required
reason: string, max 200                    # required
order_id: string | null                    # required key, null allowed
tags: list[enum[...]]                      # optional, default []
```

You do **not** make `label` a free string "so we can grow". You add a label by changing the enum and shipping a version. Nested: if you need a citation, `{source_id, quote}` is an object, not `"source_id: quote"` in a string.

Generate OpenAPI / JSON Schema from the same model your handler imports. The vendor flag gets that schema. The parser gets that schema. The UI gets the type.

## Failure modes

1. **Everything optional.** The model omits the only field you needed. You cannot tell "not applicable" from "forgot".

2. **Stringly enums.** `label: string`. You will get `Billing`, `bill`, and `not sure`.

3. **Nested data as a string.** JSON-in-JSON. You threw away the constraint.

4. **Two schemas.** Vendor copy drifted from Pydantic. Local validate passes; the UI type lies.

## How you would defend it in a review

Open the schema. If every field is an optional string, send it back. Ask whether vendor, validator, and app types are generated from one model. Two pasted copies fail the review.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Schemas are contracts: required vs optional, enums, lists, nested objects.
- One schema should drive vendor, validator, and application types.
- Closed sets are enums, not free-form strings.
- Optional means absent is legal; required-and-null is a different story.
- Do not encode nested records as strings.
- Adding a label is a schema version, not a hope the model invents one.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The model returns `label: "not sure"` and your UI crashes. What was missing? An enum (and a planned escape like other). A free-form string invited a value the UI did not handle. Tighten the schema and map unknown values in a repair step if you must. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When do you use required-key-plus-null instead of optional? When you need the model to decide 'I looked and there is no order id' rather than omitting the key. Absence and null mean different things to a parser and a UI. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What belongs in a production JSON schema for a classifier? A required enum for the label, a required reason string, explicit optional fields with types, and any nested objects (not encoded strings). The same model should be used locally and sent to the vendor. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I define one typed schema with required fields, enums, lists, and nested objects, and I share it across the vendor constraint, local validation, and the app type. Optional is a decision, not a default.
keyPoints: Schemas are contracts: required vs optional, enums, lists, nested objects.
One schema should drive vendor, validator, and application types.
Closed sets are enums, not free-form strings.
Optional means absent is legal; required-and-null is a different story.
Do not encode nested records as strings.
Adding a label is a schema version, not a hope the model invents one.

questions.a: A required enum for the label, a required reason string, explicit optional fields with types, and any nested objects (not encoded strings). The same model should be used locally and sent to the vendor.

questions.q: The model returns `label: "not sure"` and your UI crashes. What was missing?
questions.a: An enum (and a planned escape like other). A free-form string invited a value the UI did not handle. Tighten the schema and map unknown values in a repair step if you must.

questions.q: When do you use required-key-plus-null instead of optional?
questions.a: When you need the model to decide 'I looked and there is no order id' rather than omitting the key. Absence and null mean different things to a parser and a UI.

questions.q: How do you keep the vendor schema and Pydantic from drifting?
questions.a: Generate one from the other, or share a JSON Schema file both consume. Do not paste a second copy into the request builder.

questions.q: Why are nested objects better than a 'details' string?
questions.a: Constraints and types apply to parts you will query (source_id, quote). A string dumps the contract and invites another ad-hoc parse.

provider-native-vs-framework-support.explain:
## What it is

You should implement structured outputs **twice in your head**: once with the **provider-native** flag (OpenAI response format, Anthropic structured output or tool, Gemini schema, …) and once with the **framework** helper (`with_structured_output`, a parser). Native is the HTTP field the vendor actually enforces. The framework is a portable call that should end up setting that field — and sometimes falls back to a tool-call or a prompt if the model cannot constrain.

Knowing both matters because the helper can silently degrade. A LangChain method might use native decoding on one model and "prompt + parse" on another. Your logs should say which path ran. If you only know the helper, you cannot explain a sudden 12% parse-fail rate after a model swap.

Native knowledge also lets you drop the framework and keep the contract.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a framework upgrade changes the fallback and nobody notices until parse errors climb. Interviewers ask you to set structured output on a raw SDK **and** on LangChain. They want to hear that the helper is not magic, and that you still locally validate. They may ask how you would check which path is active: read the request, or a debug flag the helper exposes.

This is the portability note from M2.3 applied to schemas.

## How it works + one small example

For each model you run, write a one-pager:

- Native mechanism (flag name).
- What the framework helper maps to.
- Fallback if native is missing (tool schema / prompt).
- How you detect the fallback in logs.

Example. Model A: helper sets `response_format=json_schema`. Parse fails = 0.4%. Model B: helper cannot use native, prompts for JSON. Parse fails = 11%. You either drop Model B, add a repair loop, or pin Model A for this feature. Without the one-pager you would have blamed "the model got worse".

Implement the native call once in a unit test that inspects the request body, so a helper upgrade cannot change it silently.

## Failure modes

1. **Helper-only knowledge.** You cannot set the flag on the raw SDK in an interview or an incident.

2. **Silent fallback to prompting.** Failures look like model quality.

3. **Different helpers, different schemas.** LangChain copy drifted from the OpenAI copy.

4. **No test on the request body.** An upgrade changed `json_object` (loose) back from `json_schema` (strict).

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which path the helper used on last week's model id: native, tool, or prompt fallback. If they do not log the path, they cannot explain a parse-rate jump. Ask for the request-body test.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Know the native flag and what the framework helper maps to.
- Helpers can silently fall back to prompt-and-parse.
- Log the path: native constraint vs tool vs prompt.
- One shared schema for both implementations.
- Assert the request body in a test so upgrades cannot loosen the flag.
- A model swap that loses native support is a product change.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Parse failures jump after you change model ids but not code. What do you check? Whether the helper still uses native constrained decoding on the new id, or fell back to prompt-and-parse. Read the request body and the fail rate, not just the prompt. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you stop a library upgrade from loosening json_schema to json_object? A unit test that builds the request and asserts the native flag and schema are present. Plus a log field for the path. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why implement structured output both natively and via a framework? So you know the HTTP field the vendor enforces, you can drop the framework, and you can tell when a helper silently falls back to prompting. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I can set structured output on the vendor flag and through the framework helper, and I log which path ran. The helper is a mapper; if it falls back to prompting I treat that as a different, weaker system.
keyPoints: Know the native flag and what the framework helper maps to.
Helpers can silently fall back to prompt-and-parse.
Log the path: native constraint vs tool vs prompt.
One shared schema for both implementations.
Assert the request body in a test so upgrades cannot loosen the flag.
A model swap that loses native support is a product change.

questions.a: So you know the HTTP field the vendor enforces, you can drop the framework, and you can tell when a helper silently falls back to prompting.

questions.q: Parse failures jump after you change model ids but not code. What do you check?
questions.a: Whether the helper still uses native constrained decoding on the new id, or fell back to prompt-and-parse. Read the request body and the fail rate, not just the prompt.

questions.q: How do you stop a library upgrade from loosening json_schema to json_object?
questions.a: A unit test that builds the request and asserts the native flag and schema are present. Plus a log field for the path.

questions.q: The interviewer hands you a raw SDK. How do you request structured output?
questions.a: Attach the vendor's schema/response-format (or a tool with a JSON schema) on the call, then parse with your local model. Do not only add 'return JSON' to the prompt.

questions.q: What should a log line say besides 'structured=true'?
questions.a: The mechanism: native schema, tool-schema, or prompt fallback. Those three have very different failure rates.

validating-before-use.explain:
## What it is

A model output is **untrusted input**. Even after constrained generation, you validate with your own schema library **before** the object touches a database, a tool, a UI state machine, or another model. Validation means: types, required keys, enums, ranges, string lengths, and any extra business predicates you can check without a human (id format, allow-listed status values).

"The vendor said it matched the schema" is not a boundary. Your process, your memory, your invariants. The validator is the same code you would use for a public HTTP request. If you would not `INSERT` a user-supplied JSON blob, you do not `INSERT` a model-supplied one.

Validation is fail-closed. A miss goes to repair or reject, not to a default that looks like a real record.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the expensive bugs are valid-looking writes: a `qty` of `-1`, a `label` the warehouse does not stock, an `email` that is three paragraphs. Interviewers will ask when you validate. "Before use" is the phrase. They want a library (zod, Pydantic), not `if 'label' in data`. They also want you to refuse to "keep going" on a partial object just because the UI is waiting.

This is the same hygiene as tool arguments in M2.5–M2.6. Structured output is still a stranger at the door.

## How it works + one small example

`raw = complete(...)` → `parsed = Schema.safe_parse(raw)` → if fail, repair or reject → if pass, **then** `db.write` / `tool(parsed)`.

Example. `{label, reason, order_id}`. Validator checks enum, reason length, and `order_id` matches `^ORD-[0-9]+$` or is null. A model returns `order_id: "please see above"`. Native constraint allowed a string; your predicate rejects. You retry once with the validator error, or you store a rejected turn, not an order row.

Do not validate only in the happy-path type (`Schema.parse` that throws in an uncaught frame). Use a result type you handle.

## Failure modes

1. **Use then validate.** You wrote the row, then the schema failed in a log line. The row is already there.

2. **`dict.get` as a validator.** Missing keys become `None` and look like real nulls.

3. **Catch-all default.** Invalid label becomes `other` without a reject event. Your metrics lie and you cannot repair.

4. **Different validator in batch vs online.** Nightly jobs write garbage the API would have refused.

## How you would defend it in a review

Find the first side effect in the handler. The validator must sit above it. dict.get as a validator is a reject. Ask whether batch uses the same function.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Model output is untrusted; validate before any side effect.
- Use a real schema library, not dict.get and hope.
- Vendor 'it matched' is not your process boundary.
- Fail closed: repair or reject, do not default into a real record.
- Business predicates (id format, ranges) belong next to types.
- Online and batch must share the same validator.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A qty of -2 reached the warehouse. Structured output was on. What was missing? A local predicate (qty > 0) before use. The schema allowed an integer; it did not allow a business-legal integer. Validate ranges, not only types. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why is dict.get('label') a bad validator? A missing key becomes None and looks like a deliberate null. You lose the required-field failure and you cannot trigger repair. Use a schema that distinguishes absent, null, and value. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: When do you validate a structured model output? Immediately after parse and before any database write, tool call, or UI commit. The vendor constraint is not sufficient. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I validate with my own schema library before any write, tool, or UI update. Vendor constraints are not a boundary. Fail closed: repair or reject, do not insert a half object.

Use a real schema library, not dict.get and hope.
Vendor 'it matched' is not your process boundary.
Fail closed: repair or reject, do not default into a real record.
Business predicates (id format, ranges) belong next to types.
Online and batch must share the same validator.

questions.a: Immediately after parse and before any database write, tool call, or UI commit. The vendor constraint is not sufficient.

questions.q: A qty of -2 reached the warehouse. Structured output was on. What was missing?
questions.a: A local predicate (qty > 0) before use. The schema allowed an integer; it did not allow a business-legal integer. Validate ranges, not only types.

questions.q: What do you do on validation failure in a user-facing turn?
questions.a: Repair once with the validator error, or reject with a safe message. Do not write a default that looks successful. Log the raw payload and the error.

questions.q: Should batch jobs use a looser schema to 'keep throughput'?
questions.a: No. Share the same validator. Garbage at night is still garbage, and it is harder to notice.

syntactic-validity-vs-semantic-correctne.explain:
## What it is

**Syntactic validity** means the bytes match the schema: keys, types, enums, required fields. **Semantic correctness** means the values are true and useful in the world: the label matches the ticket, the `order_id` exists, the date is not last century, the citation actually supports the claim. Valid JSON can be confidently wrong. This split is the whole reason you still evaluate after you parse.

A lot of production dashboards only track parse rate. That number can be 100% while half the labels are inverted. Syntax is a gate. Semantics need a golden set, a database lookup, or a human/judge.

Constrained decoding raises parse rate. It does nothing to semantics except sometimes *hurt* them if a tight enum forces a guess instead of abstention.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, PMs will celebrate "we got JSON working" and ship. Support then files tickets about wrong refunds that looked perfectly structured. Interviewers will hand you a valid object with a nonsense `order_id` and ask if you are done. "No — syntax passed, meaning is unchecked" is the line. They want one concrete semantic check (exists in DB, enum matches a retrieved policy, judge on a held-out set).

This note is also how you talk about hallucinations without the word becoming mush. A hallucinated id that passes JSON Schema is the example.

## How it works + one small example

Put two boxes on the board.

Syntax: schema validate. Fail → repair/reject.
Semantics: cheap checks first (id exists, date range, foreign key), then sampled evals (golden set, judge).

Example. `{order_id: "ORD-99", status: "shipped"}` parses. `ORD-99` is not in the orders table, or it is `cancelled`. Syntax passed; semantics failed. You do not tell the user it shipped. You look up the id, and if missing you abstain or repair.

A second example: label enum is valid `billing` but the ticket is a password reset. Only a labelled set or a second reviewer catches that. Track **both** rates: parse_ok and task_ok.

## Failure modes

1. **Parse rate as the KPI.** You optimise the decoder and miss the task.

2. **No cheap semantic checks.** You never look up ids you emit.

3. **Forcing an enum with no abstain.** The model must pick a label; syntax is perfect; meaning is a coin flip on edge cases.

4. **Judging only fluent English.** The JSON is valid and the sentence is pretty. The id is still invented.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for parse_ok and task_ok as separate numbers. If they only have parse rate, the feature is not evaluated. Ask which emitted ids are looked up before the user sees them.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Syntax: schema match. Semantics: true and useful in the world.
- Constrained decoding lifts parse rate, not task accuracy.
- Look up emitted ids and other cheap facts before you speak them.
- Track parse_ok and task_ok as different metrics.
- A tight enum without abstain can force a wrong but valid guess.
- Fluent, valid output can still be a hallucination.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Parse rate is 99.9% but users complain about wrong labels. What did you measure? Only syntax. Add a golden set or cheap lookups and track task accuracy separately. Do not tighten the decoder further and call it done. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What is a cheap semantic check you can run on every turn? Primary-key existence, allow-listed statuses, date ranges, and enum membership against the live catalogue — anything a database or config can confirm without a judge. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Give an example of syntactically valid, semantically wrong output. A schema-valid {order_id, status: shipped} where the id does not exist or the order is cancelled. JSON parsed; the world disagrees. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Valid JSON is syntax. Correctness is whether the values are true. I track both, I look up ids I emit, and I never treat a 100% parse rate as a finished feature.
keyPoints: Syntax: schema match. Semantics: true and useful in the world.
Constrained decoding lifts parse rate, not task accuracy.
Look up emitted ids and other cheap facts before you speak them.
Track parse_ok and task_ok as different metrics.
A tight enum without abstain can force a wrong but valid guess.
Fluent, valid output can still be a hallucination.

questions.a: If every field is required and there is no abstain/other, the model must emit a valid-looking guess instead of refusing. Add an explicit unknown path.

questions.q: Why is 'it returned JSON' a weak launch criterion?
questions.a: JSON is the envelope. Launch needs a measured task_ok on a held-out set, plus the cheap lookups that stop invented ids.

generate-validate-repair.explain:
## What it is

The production loop for structured output is **generate → validate → accept / retry / repair / reject**. Generate under a schema. Validate locally. If it passes, accept. If it fails, you have three honest exits: **retry** the same call (rare; only for transient vendor errors), **repair** once by sending the validator error back to the model, or **reject** with a safe fallback that cannot be mistaken for a successful record.

Repair is a second, bounded call: "Your previous object failed: `order_id` is not ORD-\d+. Return a corrected object." It is not an unbounded conversation with the parser. After one (at most two) repairs, you reject. Reject means a default the product designed (`other`, `insufficient`, an empty list) plus a log, not a guessed record.

This loop is also where finish_reason=`length` goes: you do not repair a truncated object by closing braces; you retry with a shorter schema or a higher cap.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this loop is the difference between a brittle demo and a feature ops can live with. Interviewers will ask you to walk generate-validate-repair and what the fallback looks like. They want a cap on repairs (cost and loops), a fallback that is obviously a fallback, and logs of every fail. "We just retry until it works" is a bill and a hang.

This is M2.4's design question, sibling to M2.9's retry map. Schema failures are usually not 503s; do not treat them like transport.

## How it works + one small example

Write it as a state machine.

1. Generate (native schema, timeout, request id).
2. If transport fail → M2.9 retry map.
3. If `length` → retry once with shorter output or higher cap; do not parse.
4. Validate. Pass → accept.
5. Fail → one repair call with the error text; validate again.
6. Still fail → reject: return the product's safe object, log raw + errors, do not write the business row.

Example. Extract `{emails: [string]}`. First object has `emails: "a@b.c, d@e.f"` (a string). Validator fails (expected list). Repair prompt includes the error. Second object is a list. Accept. If the second is still a string, reject to `emails: []` and a `rejected=true` flag the UI can show.

## Failure modes

1. **Unbounded repair.** The model and the parser argue for ten turns. You pay and you delay the user.

2. **Fallback that looks successful.** Invalid label becomes `billing` because it is the first enum. You shipped a lie.

3. **Repairing `length` with a brace-closer.** You invent fields. Reject or retry the generation.

4. **No log of the fail.** You cannot see that repair rate is 40% and the schema is too tight or the model is too weak.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask how many repairs are allowed and what the reject object looks like. Unbounded retry-until-valid is a reject. Ask how length is handled — closing braces is a fail.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Loop: generate → validate → accept, retry, repair, or reject.
- Repair at most once or twice with the validator error; then stop.
- Reject with a designed safe object, not a guessed valid one.
- Do not treat schema fails like 503s; do not treat length as parseable.
- Log raw payload and validator errors so repair rate is visible.
- Transport retries and schema repairs are different maps.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Repair has run four times and the object is still invalid. What should have happened? You should have rejected after one or two repairs. Unbounded repair burns tokens and time. Log the raw failures and fix the schema or the model, do not loop. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What is a safe reject for a classifier versus a dangerous one? Safe: other or insufficient_evidence with a flag. Dangerous: picking the first enum value or a guessed label that looks like success. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Walk the generate → validate → repair loop and its exits. Generate under a schema, validate locally. Accept if it passes. On schema fail, repair once by sending the validator error. If that fails, reject to a designed fallback. Transport errors use a separate retry map. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Generate under a schema, validate locally, repair once with the error, then accept or reject. The fallback must look like a fallback. I never close truncated JSON myself and I never retry forever.
keyPoints: Loop: generate → validate → accept, retry, repair, or reject.
Repair at most once or twice with the validator error; then stop.
Reject with a designed safe object, not a guessed valid one.
Do not treat schema fails like 503s; do not treat length as parseable.
Log raw payload and validator errors so repair rate is visible.
Transport retries and schema repairs are different maps.

questions.a: Generate under a schema, validate locally. Accept if it passes. On schema fail, repair once by sending the validator error. If that fails, reject to a designed fallback. Transport errors use a separate retry map.
