questions.a: You should have rejected after one or two repairs. Unbounded repair burns tokens and time. Log the raw failures and fix the schema or the model, do not loop.

questions.q: What is a safe reject for a classifier versus a dangerous one?
questions.a: Safe: other or insufficient_evidence with a flag. Dangerous: picking the first enum value or a guessed label that looks like success.

questions.a: No. Do not close braces. Retry generation with a shorter output or a higher cap, or reject. Repair is for complete-but-invalid objects.

questions.q: Why log repair rate as its own metric?
questions.a: A high repair rate means the schema, the model, or the prompt is wrong. If you only log final success, you hide the cost and the fragility.

enum-and-optional-fields-in-schemas.explain:
## What it is

Tight types are how you stop a parser from "succeeding" on mush. An **enum** is a closed set the model must pick from (`billing | bug | how-to | other`). An **optional field** is a key that may be absent; if present it still has a type. A free-form string is what you use when the value is truly open (a reason sentence), not when you were too lazy to list the cases.

Enums belong on labels, statuses, countries, reason codes — anything you will `switch` on. Optional belongs on information that is allowed to be missing (`phone` on a lead). Required-plus-null belongs on "we asked and the answer is none" (`order_id`). Mixing these three is how APIs become unreadable.

The model sees enum values in the schema. Keep them stable, documented, and short. Do not put a 2_000-word policy in an enum description.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, every free-form field you later parse with if-else is a schema you refused to write. Interviewers will ask you to tighten a sloppy schema. They want enums on closed sets, optionals that are intentional, and the sentence "tight types beat a string the parser cannot trust". They also want an escape enum (`other`, `unknown`) so tightness does not force a lie.

This is the most practical schema skill in the module. It shows up in every take-home.

## How it works + one small example

Rewrite a bad extractor.

Before: `{ "type": string, "id": string, "extra": string }`.
After: `{ "type": enum[order, ticket, unknown], "id": string | null, "priority": enum[low, med, high] | omitted }`.

You add `unknown` so the model is not forced to pick `order`. You keep `reason` as a string because it is open text. You do not add `extra` as a junk drawer.

When the set grows, you version the schema (`label_v2`) or you add a value and ship the UI the same day. You do not silently accept old clients sending free text.

## Failure modes

1. **Enum without an escape.** Edge cases become random valid values.

2. **Optional everything.** You cannot require the one field you need.

3. **Junk-drawer strings.** `extra`, `notes`, `raw` — the model dumps structure there.

4. **Enums that change daily.** You are using an enum for an open catalogue; retrieve the catalogue instead.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to tighten one free-form field into an enum with an escape. If they argue they might need new values, ask how they will version the schema. A junk-drawer extra string fails.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Enums for closed sets; strings for truly open text.
- Always include an escape (other/unknown) on forced choices.
- Optional vs required-plus-null are different meanings.
- Tight types beat a free-form string you will parse again.
- No junk-drawer fields that swallow structure.
- Version the schema when the enum changes; do not silently loosen.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The model must pick a ticket type and has no 'other'. What goes wrong? Edge cases become a random valid type. Syntax stays perfect; semantics rot. Add other/unknown or make the field nullable with a reason. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Tighten {type: string, extra: string} for an order-or-ticket extractor. type as enum[order, ticket, unknown], id as string|null, drop extra or replace it with typed optional fields. Keep a separate reason string if you need open text. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: When should a field be an enum rather than a string? When your code will branch on a closed set of values (labels, statuses, reason codes). If you would write a switch, write an enum — plus an escape value. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Closed sets are enums with an escape hatch. Optional is deliberate. I do not leave a free-form string where I will later write a switch, because the parser cannot trust it.
keyPoints: Enums for closed sets; strings for truly open text.
Always include an escape (other/unknown) on forced choices.
Optional vs required-plus-null are different meanings.
Tight types beat a free-form string you will parse again.
No junk-drawer fields that swallow structure.
Version the schema when the enum changes; do not silently loosen.

questions.q: When should a field be an enum rather than a string?
questions.a: When your code will branch on a closed set of values (labels, statuses, reason codes). If you would write a switch, write an enum — plus an escape value.

questions.q: The model must pick a ticket type and has no 'other'. What goes wrong?
questions.a: Edge cases become a random valid type. Syntax stays perfect; semantics rot. Add other/unknown or make the field nullable with a reason.

questions.q: Tighten {type: string, extra: string} for an order-or-ticket extractor.

questions.q: The catalogue of product SKUs changes hourly. Should SKU be an enum?
questions.a: No. That is an open, moving set. Use a string plus a lookup against the live catalogue (semantic check), not an enum you cannot ship hourly.

questions.a: Omit (optional) means the field was not in scope. Null (required key) means we asked and there is no priority. Pick one meaning and document it.

what-to-do-when-the-model-omits-a-field.explain:
## What it is

When a required field is missing, you have two honest moves: **default in code** (only if the default is safe and designed) or **retry once with the validator error**. You do not invent a business value, and you do not silently treat missing as null unless the schema said that was legal.

"Default in code" is for true product defaults: `tags=[]`, `notify=false`, `language="en"` when the product already treats those as implicit. It is not for `label=billing` or `amount=0`. Those are guesses. "Retry once" is the repair step: show the model which key failed and what the type was. After that, reject.

Optional fields that are omitted are not errors. Required fields that are omitted are. Do not blur them in the handler.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, omitted fields are how half-records enter the warehouse. Interviewers will ask "the model dropped `order_id`, what do you do?". They want: if it was optional, continue; if required, repair once or default only when the default is harmless; never fabricate an id. They also want you to log the omit so you can see a model or schema problem.

This is a small note with a high signal. It shows you will not "just fill it in".

## How it works + one small example

Validator returns `{missing: ["order_id"]}`.

- If `order_id` is optional: accept; UI shows "no id".
- If required and a safe default exists (it does not, for ids): do not default.
- Repair once: "order_id is required and must match ORD-\d+ or be null".
- Still missing: reject the turn. Store the raw object. Show a fallback card.

Example. `notify` omitted, schema optional, product default false. You default in code and log `defaulted=notify`. Example 2. `label` omitted, schema required. You repair once; if it is still gone, you return `other` **only if** `other` is the designed reject, and you flag `rejected=true`.

Do not write `data["label"] = data.get("label") or "billing"`.

## Failure modes

1. **Guessing a business field.** Missing label becomes the popular class. Metrics look healthy.

2. **Treating required as optional at the handler.** The schema said required; the code shrugged.

3. **Defaulting an id to a placeholder.** `ORD-0000` later joins a real row or confuses support.

4. **Repair loops on a field the model cannot know.** If the ticket has no id, the schema should allow null; stop asking for a miracle.

## How you would defend it in a review

Ask what happens when a required key is missing. A default that invents a label or an id is a reject. Ask them to distinguish optional omit from required omit in the handler.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Required omit: repair once or a designed safe default; then reject.
- Optional omit is not an error.
- Never invent ids, amounts, or labels as defaults.
- Empty lists and false flags can be real product defaults — log them.
- If the model cannot know the value, the schema should allow null.
- Do not bypass required in the handler with dict.get.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A handler writes label = data.get('label') or 'billing'. Why is that a bug? It turns a missing required field into a guessed business value. Metrics and users see a real label. Repair or reject instead. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When is defaulting in code acceptable? When the product already has a safe implicit value (tags=[], notify=false, language=en) and you log that you defaulted. Not for identifiers, money, or class labels. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: The model omits a required order_id. What are the legal next steps? Retry once with the validator error (repair), or reject. Do not invent an id or silently treat the key as optional. If many tickets have no id, change the schema to allow null. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

If a required field is missing I repair once with the validator error, or I apply a designed safe default. I never invent a business value, and I treat optional omits as legal.
keyPoints: Required omit: repair once or a designed safe default; then reject.
Optional omit is not an error.
Never invent ids, amounts, or labels as defaults.
Empty lists and false flags can be real product defaults — log them.
If the model cannot know the value, the schema should allow null.
Do not bypass required in the handler with dict.get.

questions.a: Retry once with the validator error (repair), or reject. Do not invent an id or silently treat the key as optional. If many tickets have no id, change the schema to allow null.

questions.q: A handler writes label = data.get('label') or 'billing'. Why is that a bug?
questions.a: It turns a missing required field into a guessed business value. Metrics and users see a real label. Repair or reject instead.

questions.q: When is defaulting in code acceptable?
questions.a: When the product already has a safe implicit value (tags=[], notify=false, language=en) and you log that you defaulted. Not for identifiers, money, or class labels.

questions.q: Repairs keep asking for a phone number the ticket never contained. What should change?
questions.a: The schema. Make phone optional or null, and stop repairing for information that is not in the input. Repair cannot create facts.

questions.q: How do you make omits visible to ops?
questions.a: Log missing keys, repair counts, and defaulted fields on the request row. A rising omit rate is a schema or model issue, not user noise.

who-chooses-and-who-executes.explain:
## What it is

Tool calling splits two jobs that people mash together. The **model chooses**: it looks at the user turn and the tool list, then emits a structured **tool request** — a name plus arguments. **Your application executes**: it validates those arguments, checks permissions, calls the real function or HTTP API, and only then sends a **tool result** back as a new message. The model cannot open a socket, refund a card, or query your database unless you run the code.

This split is the whole security model. A tool request is a suggestion, not a syscall. Treat it like an untrusted HTTP body from the public internet. The model is a planner with a form; you are the process that may submit that form.

Providers differ on names (function call, tool use, tool_calls) and on whether multiple calls arrive in one turn. The split does not change.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the first dangerous bug is executing whatever the model asked. Interviewers will ask who calls the refund function. If you say the model, you failed. The senior line is: the model proposes, my code authorises and executes, I return a result, the model writes the user-facing sentence. They also want you to say that a well-written description changes what the model proposes, but never replaces the authorisation check.

This is the most important sentence in Level 2 after 'the API is stateless'.

## How it works + one small example

Draw four boxes: User → Model → Your executor → Model.

Example. User: 'Cancel order ORD-9 and refund me.' The model emits `refund(order_id=ORD-9, amount=full)`. Your executor: (1) parse and schema-validate, (2) load ORD-9 for this user, (3) refuse if not theirs or already refunded, (4) call billing, (5) return `{ok: true, amount: 1400}` as a tool message. The model then says 'Refunded ₹1,400.' If you had executed blindly, a hallucinated order id or a stranger's id would have moved money.

The model never sees your billing API key. It sees a result payload you chose to send.

## Failure modes

1. **Executing the proposal as a syscall.** No auth, no id check. This is the incident.

2. **Letting the model call HTTP itself** (unconstrained browsing or a shell). You gave away the split.

3. **Returning stack traces to the model.** It will echo them to the user or retry destructively. Return a short, structured error.

4. **Confusing 'the SDK ran the tool' with 'we authorised it'.** A framework executor that just `fn(**args)` is still your process — you still owe the checks.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask the author to draw the four boxes and to point at the authorisation line in the executor. If the model output is piped into a function with star-args and no user check, the review is a reject. Ask what the model sees if billing throws.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- The model chooses a tool and arguments; your app executes.
- A tool request is untrusted input, not a syscall.
- Authorise against the current user before any side effect.
- Return a short structured result, not a stack trace.
- Framework 'auto execute' does not remove your checks.
- The model never holds the downstream API key.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A framework offers auto-execute=true. What is still your job? The same validation and authorisation. Auto-execute only means the framework will call your function pointer. It is not an approval step. Then show the change you would ship the same week. The model asks to refund ORD-9. What must your executor do before calling billing? Parse and schema-validate, load the order for the current user, refuse if missing, not theirs, or already refunded, then call billing. Return a structured result. Do not execute the proposal blindly. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Who chooses a tool, and who executes it? The model usually chooses the tool and generates arguments. Your application validates, authorises, executes the real function, and returns a result message. The model cannot perform the side effect by itself. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The model proposes a tool name and arguments. My code validates, authorises, executes, and returns a result. The model never touches the side effect directly.
keyPoints: The model chooses a tool and arguments; your app executes.
A tool request is untrusted input, not a syscall.
Authorise against the current user before any side effect.
Return a short structured result, not a stack trace.
Framework 'auto execute' does not remove your checks.
The model never holds the downstream API key.

questions.a: The model usually chooses the tool and generates arguments. Your application validates, authorises, executes the real function, and returns a result message. The model cannot perform the side effect by itself.

questions.a: Parse and schema-validate, load the order for the current user, refuse if missing, not theirs, or already refunded, then call billing. Return a structured result. Do not execute the proposal blindly.

questions.a: The same validation and authorisation. Auto-execute only means the framework will call your function pointer. It is not an approval step.

questions.q: Why must the model not hold the billing API key?
questions.a: Anything in the prompt or in a tool the model can call without your checks can leak or be replayed. The key stays in your executor. The model sees only the result you return.

questions.q: What do you return if the tool throws?
questions.a: A short structured error the model can use (not_found, denied, retryable), not a stack trace or an HTML page. Then decide whether the model may retry or must apologise.

defining-a-tool.explain:
## What it is

A tool the model can choose is a **spec**: a **name**, a **description**, a **parameter schema** (types, required arguments, enums), and sometimes a few examples of when not to call it. The spec is what the model reads. The Python function is what you run. If they disagree, the model will fill the spec and your function will crash — or worse, do the wrong thing.

Good names are verbs plus an object (`get_order`, `create_refund`), not `do_stuff` or `api`. Good descriptions say when to use the tool, when not to, and what the arguments mean in one or two sentences. Good schemas are the same tight contracts as M2.4: enums, required keys, no junk-drawer strings.

The spec is also context. Every tool you attach spends tokens and attention on every turn. A bloated catalogue is a quality problem, not just a docs problem.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, bad specs are why the model calls `search` when it should call `get_order`. Interviewers will hand you a sloppy tool and ask you to rewrite it. They want a precise name, a description a stranger could implement, a minimal parameter list, and types that can be validated. They also want you to mention that the description is in the prompt.

This is the design skill that M2.6 deepens. Here you learn the fields; there you learn the failure modes of overlapping tools.

## How it works + one small example

Write the spec before the function.

Example. `get_order(order_id: string matching ORD-\d+)` — description: 'Fetch one order the current user owns. Use when the user names an order id. Do not use for lists or refunds.' Required: `order_id`. No `user_id` argument — you will take that from the session.

A bad spec: `order(query: string)` described as 'does orders'. The model will dump the whole user sentence into `query`. You will then parse it again, badly.

Put the JSON Schema on the wire. Share it with the local validator. Keep the description under a few hundred tokens unless you have measured that more helps.

## Failure modes

1. **Name and function disagree.** Spec says `amount` is dollars; function treats it as cents.

2. **Optional everything.** The model omits the only id you need.

3. **A string query that re-implements the schema.** You hid the types.

4. **Passing user_id as an argument.** The model can swap it. Bind identity from the session.


## How you would defend it in a review

Open the spec in the PR. If you cannot implement the function from the name, description, and types alone, send it back. Ask why any identity field is an argument. Ask how many tokens the whole tool list adds to every turn.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- A tool spec is name, description, and a typed parameter schema.
- Names are verbs plus objects; descriptions say when and when not.
- Share the schema with local validation; do not drift.
- Do not take user_id from the model; bind it from the session.
- Every attached tool costs tokens and attention each turn.
- A single query string is usually a refused schema.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Why is user_id a bad tool argument? The model can put any id there. Identity must come from the authenticated session in your executor. The tool should only take the resource id it needs. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Rewrite a tool named helper with a query string for fetching one order. get_order with required order_id (typed or patterned), a description that says it fetches one owned order and is not a search or a refund, and no catch-all query string. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What fields belong on a tool the model will choose? A precise name, a description of when to use and when not to, and a parameter schema with types and required arguments. Those fields are what the model sees. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A tool is a name, a description, and a tight parameter schema the model can read. I write the spec so a stranger could implement it, I bind identity from the session, and I share the schema with the validator.

Names are verbs plus objects; descriptions say when and when not.
Share the schema with local validation; do not drift.
Do not take user_id from the model; bind it from the session.
Every attached tool costs tokens and attention each turn.
A single query string is usually a refused schema.

questions.a: The model will send 14.00 and you will charge 14 cents, or the reverse. Align spec, validator, and function from one schema, and add a unit test on a real number.

questions.q: Why keep descriptions short unless you have measured otherwise?
questions.a: They sit in the prompt on every turn. Long, overlapping blurbs waste tokens and confuse selection. Measure if a longer description actually lifts tool-choice accuracy.

the-full-tool-calling-loop.explain:
## What it is

The loop is a protocol, not a vibe: **user → model → tool request → your execute → tool result message → model → final answer** (or another tool request). You must persist every hop. The second model call is a new HTTP request that includes the original messages, the assistant tool-call message, and your tool result. Forgetting any piece makes the model invent a result or repeat the call.

Some turns need two or three tools, or the same tool twice. The loop repeats until the model emits a normal assistant message (or you hit a cap). You own the cap. An unbounded loop is a bill and a hang.

Streaming complicates the middle: you accumulate the tool-call fragments, parse once, execute, then start the next completion. You do not stream the tool result to the user as if it were the answer.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, most 'the tool did not work' bugs are a broken loop: the result was not appended, the call id did not match, or you showed the first assistant message (the tool request) as if it were English. Interviewers will ask you to draw the loop from memory. They want the boxes, the second model call, and a max-iterations number. They will ding a diagram that stops at execute.

This is the Level 2 diagram you should be able to redraw in 90 seconds.

## How it works + one small example

Implement a `while steps < MAX` (MAX of 4 is a sane default for a support bot):

1. `resp = complete(messages, tools)`
2. If text and no tool calls: return text.
3. If tool calls: for each, execute (or in parallel if independent), append assistant tool-call message, append tool results with matching ids.
4. Loop.

Example. User asks for order status plus a refund policy. First completion: `get_order` and `get_policy`. You run both, append two results, call again. Second completion: a sentence. You stop. If the second completion asks for `get_order` again, you may return the cached result or increment the step counter and refuse a third identical call.

Log each hop with the same request/trace id.

## Failure modes

1. **Dropping the tool result.** The next completion has no evidence and hallucinates.

2. **Showing the tool-call JSON to the user.** They see `{"name":"get_order"...}` in the bubble.

3. **No MAX.** A confused model cycles tools until the budget dies.

4. **One shared result for two call ids.** The model mixes which answer belongs to which request.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask the author to write MAX on the board and to show the messages array after execute. If the tool result is not in that array, the loop is broken. Ask what the UI renders after the first completion.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- The loop is user → model → execute → result → model → answer.
- The second call must include the assistant tool-call and your result.
- Cap iterations; unbounded loops are a bill.
- Match results to tool-call ids.
- Do not show the tool-request JSON as the answer.
- Log every hop on one trace id.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The model repeats the same tool three times and never answers. What did you forget? A max-iteration cap and, probably, a clear tool result. Stop the loop, return a safe message, and log the cycle. Also check the result was actually appended with the right id. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What must the second complete() include? The original messages, the assistant message that contained the tool calls, and one tool result per call id. Omitting any of those makes the model guess. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Draw the happy-path tool loop in words. User message, model returns a tool request, your code executes and appends a tool result with the matching id, you call the model again with the full list, the model returns the user-facing answer. Repeat if more tools are requested, up to a cap. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

User, model, tool request, my execute, tool result, model again, final text. I persist every hop, I cap the loop, and I never treat the first tool-call message as the user-visible answer.

The second call must include the assistant tool-call and your result.
Cap iterations; unbounded loops are a bill.
Match results to tool-call ids.
Do not show the tool-request JSON as the answer.
Log every hop on one trace id.

tool-call-ids-returning-results.explain:
## What it is

Each tool request carries an **id** (and a name). Your result message must include **that same id** so the model can attach the result to the request it made. Parallel calls make this non-negotiable: two `get_order` calls with different arguments are distinguished only by id. Providers reject or mis-associate results that have the wrong id, a missing id, or a result with no matching request.

The result is a role (`tool` / `function`) plus content you control. Keep it small and structured. Do not dump a 40k HTML page. Do not omit the id because 'there was only one call'. The next turn may have two.

When you persist history, persist the ids. A replay or a retry that regenerates ids will orphan the stored results.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, 'the model ignored the tool' is often a mismatched id after a refactor, a streaming stitch bug, or a LangChain adapter that renamed the field. Interviewers will ask how you return a result. They want the id, the role, and the sentence that parallel calls require one result per id. They may ask what you store for audit: the id, the name, the arguments you actually executed (after validation), and the result.

## How it works + one small example

After execute:

```
messages.append(assistant_tool_call_message)  # includes id=call_abc
messages.append({role: tool, tool_call_id: call_abc, content: json.dumps(result)})
```

Example. Two calls: `call_1 get_order(ORD-1)`, `call_2 get_order(ORD-2)`. You return two tool messages. Swap the ids and the model will cite ORD-1's status for ORD-2.

On a retry of the *model* call, reuse the stored results and their ids; do not re-execute. On a retry that re-asks the model from scratch, new ids will arrive — do not attach old results to new ids.

## Failure modes

1. **One result, two calls.** The second request is answered with silence or a guess.

2. **Reusing an old id after a new completion.** The vendor 400s or the model ignores you.

3. **Huge results.** You blow the window and the next completion is garbage.

4. **String-matching on tool name only.** Two get_order calls collapse.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see a fixture with two parallel get_order calls and the exact messages appended. If results are keyed only by tool name, reject. Ask what happens to those ids on a retry.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Match each result to the tool-call id the model generated.
- Parallel calls to the same tool are distinguished by id, not name.
- Persist ids with history; do not regenerate them on replay.
- Keep result payloads small and structured.
- Do not attach an old result to a new completion's ids.
- Audit the id, the executed args, and the result together.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Two get_order calls come back; you return one combined blob. What goes wrong? The model cannot tell which status belongs to which id. Return one result message per call id, even if you executed them in one batch internally. Then show the change you would ship the same week. You retry a timed-out model call that had already produced tool calls you executed. What ids do you use? Reuse the stored assistant tool-call message and the stored results with their original ids. Do not re-execute, and do not mint new ids for old results. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why do tool results need the model's call id? So the model can pair each result with the request it made. Names are not unique when the same tool is called twice. Wrong or missing ids cause ignores or vendor 400s. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every tool result carries the exact call id the model issued. I return one result per id, I keep payloads small, and I never attach a stored result to a newly generated id.

Audit the id, the executed args, and the result together.

provider-apis-vs-langchain-tools.explain:
## What it is

You should implement tool calling on the **raw provider API** and know how **LangChain** represents the same loop. Raw: you send a `tools` array (JSON Schema), you read `tool_calls` on the assistant message, you execute, you append `role=tool` messages, you call again. LangChain: you bind tools (`bind_tools` / `@tool`), you get `AIMessage.tool_calls`, you run a `ToolNode` or your own executor, you append `ToolMessage`s. Underneath, it is the same protocol.

The framework can hide the second HTTP call inside `create_agent` or an executor. That is convenience. You still must know it happens, still must cap it, still must validate arguments. If you only know the decorator, you cannot debug a missing ToolMessage.

Portability note: tool-call JSON shape differs slightly by vendor. The adapter translates. When it fails, you read the raw request.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you will inherit both styles, sometimes in one repo. Interviewers will ask you to write the raw loop on a whiteboard and then say how LangChain wraps it. They want the mapping, not a brand. They will also ask when to skip the executor abstraction: when you need custom auth, custom parallelism, or a clearer trace.

This is M2.3's raw-vs-library comparison applied to tools.

## How it works + one small example

Write the raw loop for `get_order` in twenty lines. Then write the LangChain version with `@tool` and an agent or a manual two-step invoke. Assert the same tests. Print both HTTP bodies once.

Example. Raw OpenAI: `tools=[{type:function, function:{name, parameters}}]`. LangChain: `model.bind_tools([get_order])`. Both should send a function schema. If LangChain sent a different required set, you found a drift; fix the shared schema.

Do not use a fully autonomous agent runner for a one-tool fetch. Manual loop is easier to cap and to auth.

## Failure modes

1. **Only knowing the decorator.** You cannot find the second call in an incident.

2. **Agent runner with no cap.** Same unbounded loop, prettier name.

3. **Schema drift** between the raw test and the LangChain tool.

4. **Assuming ToolNode authorises.** It calls your function; you still check the user.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to write the raw messages array on the board, then the LangChain equivalents. If they cannot find the second HTTP call in the framework path, they do not own the loop. Ask where auth lives.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Raw API and LangChain implement the same propose-execute-return protocol.
- Know where the second HTTP call lives in both styles.
- Share one schema; do not let the decorator drift from the raw test.
- A ToolNode is an executor, not an authoriser.
- Skip an agent runner when a manual two-step loop is enough.
- Read the raw request when the adapter mis-shapes a tool.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. An agent executor spins on one tool for a minute. What do you check? The iteration cap, whether ToolMessages were appended, and whether your function is throwing in a way the agent interprets as retry. Then consider replacing the executor with a manual loop you can see. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When would you refuse create_agent for a feature? One or two known tools, a required auth check, and a need for a short trace. A manual loop is fewer moving parts. Use an agent runner when the graph is actually unknown. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Map a raw tool loop onto LangChain objects. tools array becomes bind_tools or @tool. Assistant tool_calls become AIMessage.tool_calls. Your execute plus role=tool becomes a ToolMessage (or ToolNode). The next complete() is the next invoke. Caps and auth stay yours. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I can write the tool loop on the provider API and map it onto LangChain's bind_tools and ToolMessage. The protocol is the same; I still validate, authorise, and cap, whichever wrapper I use.

Share one schema; do not let the decorator drift from the raw test.
A ToolNode is an executor, not an authoriser.
Skip an agent runner when a manual two-step loop is enough.
Read the raw request when the adapter mis-shapes a tool.

sequential-repeated-parallel-calls.explain:
## What it is

Models will ask for tools in three patterns you must handle. **Sequential**: the second call needs the first result (`get_order` then `refund` with the amount you just fetched). **Repeated**: the same tool twice with different arguments (`get_order` for ORD-1 and ORD-2). **Parallel**: several independent calls in one assistant message, which you can execute concurrently.

A fourth pattern is **dynamic**: the model decides the next tool after seeing a result. That is still your loop with a cap, not an excuse to drop authorisation. Frameworks that 'run tools in parallel' will happily parallelise two refunds you wanted sequenced. You decide which names are parallel-safe.

Independence is a property of **side effects**, not of names. Two reads are usually parallel-safe. Two writes often are not.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a parallel refund-plus-cancel can race. A sequential assumption that you always execute in list order can add 800ms for two independent reads. Interviewers will ask how you handle multiple tool_calls in one message. They want: match by id, parallelise only if side-effect safe, sequence when the second needs the first, and never assume the SDK order is a transaction.

They may also ask what you do if one parallel arm fails: fail the turn, or return the success plus a structured error for the failed id.

## How it works + one small example

Classify tools at registration: `read` vs `write`. Reads in one message → `asyncio.gather` with a bound. Writes → sequential, or refuse to run two writes in one turn without an explicit workflow.

Example. Message has `get_order(ORD-1)` and `get_policy(refund)`. Parallel. Next message has `refund(ORD-1)` — sequential after the user (or you) confirmed. If a message ever contains two `refund`s, run them sequentially under one lock per order id, or reject and ask the model to do one.

Repeated `get_order` with the same id in one turn: return the cached result for the second id rather than hitting the DB twice, still as two tool messages.

## Failure modes

1. **Parallel writes.** Double charge, last-write-wins, or a partial cancel.

2. **Forcing everything sequential.** p95 dies on independent reads.

3. **One failure kills the silent others.** You drop a successful get_order because get_policy 500'd, and the model retries both.

4. **Treating list order as a transaction.** It is not atomic unless you make it so.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which tools are marked write and whether two of them can run in one gather. If the answer is yes, reject. Ask to see one-failure fixtures: one arm 500, the other 200.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Handle sequential, repeated, and parallel tool calls on purpose.
- Parallelise only side-effect-safe (usually reads).
- Sequence or lock writes; list order is not a transaction.
- One result per id even if an arm fails.
- Repeated identical reads can reuse a cache but still return two messages.
- Register tools as read or write so the executor can decide.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. One of two parallel reads fails. What do you send the model? A success result for the id that worked and a structured error for the id that failed. Do not invent the missing payload and do not hide the success. Then show the change you would ship the same week. A single assistant message contains two get_order calls and one refund. How do you run them? Run the two reads concurrently (or sequentially if you prefer), do not run the refund in parallel with anything that touches the same order, then return three results keyed by id. Prefer refusing a write bundled with unrelated work if you cannot reason about the race. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why is executing tool_calls in array order not enough for writes? Order is not atomicity. Two writes can still overlap with other requests. Use a per-resource lock or a real workflow, and do not assume the model intended a transaction. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I match calls by id, I parallelise independent reads, I sequence writes, and I return one result per id even when one arm fails. Parallel is a side-effect decision, not a default.

tool-failures-malformed-arguments.explain:
## What it is

The model will send **malformed arguments** and tools will **fail**. Your executor must assume both. Malformed: missing keys, wrong types, extra keys, strings that do not match a pattern, an enum you do not have. Failed: timeouts, 404s, 409s, permission denials, downstream 500s. None of these should crash the worker or look like a successful side effect.

Handle malformed **before** the side effect: schema validate, then business-validate (id exists, user owns it). Return a structured error the model can correct (`invalid_args`, with the validator text) or stop the loop if the model is repeating the same bad args. Handle tool failures **after** you tried: map them to `not_found`, `denied`, `retryable`, `fatal`. Only `retryable` is a candidate for one automatic retry — of the **tool**, not of a write you are unsure about.

Never assume an invocation is executable because the model asked.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, an unhandled exception in a tool turns a chat into a 500 page, or worse, a retry that double-writes. Interviewers will ask what you do with bad arguments. They want validate-then-refuse, not a crash, and they want the model to see a short error rather than a stack trace. They will also ask whether you retry a 500 from billing: once, idempotently, and never on a 409 that says already refunded.

## How it works + one small example

Executor skeleton:

1. Parse JSON (after the stream completes).
2. Schema validate → on fail, return `invalid_args` + messages, do not call the API.
3. Business validate (exists, ACL) → on fail, return `denied` or `not_found`.
4. Call the API with a timeout and an idempotency key for writes.
5. Map the outcome to a small object.

Example. Args `{order_id: "please"}`. Schema fails. You do not hit billing. The model may repair. Second try `{order_id: "ORD-9"}` but ORD-9 is another user's. You return `denied` without leaking that the order exists if your policy says so. A 503 from billing: one retry with the same idempotency key, then `retryable` to the model or a human handoff.

## Failure modes

1. **Crashing the worker** on parse errors. One bad argument takes down the chat process.

2. **Retrying a 409 already-refunded.** You confuse the model and the user.

3. **Echoing raw downstream HTML.** Prompt injection and leaked internals.

4. **Treating invalid_args as a vendor 503.** You apply the wrong retry map.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see the invalid_args path and a 409 path in tests. If unhandled exceptions escape the executor, reject. Ask which writes have an idempotency key.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Validate arguments before the side effect; never assume they are executable.
- Map tool failures to not_found, denied, retryable, or fatal.
- Do not crash the worker on parse errors.
- Retry writes only with an idempotency key; do not retry 409s.
- Return short structured errors, never stack traces or HTML.
- invalid_args is a schema problem, not a transport 503.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Billing returns 409 already refunded. Should you retry? No. Return a structured already_done to the model and treat the user-facing outcome as success-or-explain, not as a transient error. Retrying a 409 can confuse ledgers. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you retry a 503 on a write tool? Once, with the same idempotency key and a timeout, then give up to the model or a human. Without a key, do not retry; you may double-write. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What do you do when tool arguments fail the schema? Do not call the downstream API. Return a structured invalid_args error with the validator text so the model can repair once. If it repeats, stop the loop. Do not crash. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I assume arguments are bad and tools fail. I validate before any side effect, I map failures to a small error object, I retry writes only when idempotent, and I never crash the worker on a bad proposal.

Do not crash the worker on parse errors.
Retry writes only with an idempotency key; do not retry 409s.
Return short structured errors, never stack traces or HTML.

tool-choice-auto-vs-required-vs-none.explain:
## What it is

Providers let you constrain **whether** a tool may be called this turn. Typical settings: **auto** (the model may call a tool or answer in text), **required** / `any` (it must call at least one tool), **none** (it must not), and sometimes a **forced function name** (it must call this one). These are turn-level policies, not permissions. `required` does not authorise a refund; it only forbids a bare-text shrug.

Use **auto** for mixed turns ('answer if you know, look up if you do not'). Use **required** when the product contract is 'this turn must hit the catalogue' — a price check, a retrieval, a form lookup. Use **none** when you want a draft or a summary and a tool would be a side-effect risk. Use a forced name when the router already decided `get_order`.

Wrong settings are common bugs: auto on a 'must look up' turn produces confident guesses; required on a chitchat turn forces a nonsense call; none on a price turn invents a number.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, tool_choice is how you stop a billing bot from estimating a price from memory. Interviewers will ask when you force a tool versus when you forbid one. They want: required when the turn is worthless without the call, none when a call would be dangerous or pointless, auto as the default, and forced name when a router already picked. They will ding 'we always use auto'.

## How it works + one small example

Set it per feature, not globally.

Example. Price quote: `tool_choice=required` (or forced `get_price`). Chitchat / 'thanks': `none`. Support answer that might need an order: `auto`. After a tool just failed with `denied`, you may set `none` on the follow-up so the model apologises instead of retrying.

Log the setting. When users say 'it guessed the price', check whether that turn was auto.

## Failure modes

1. **Global auto.** Price turns hallucinate.

2. **Global required.** 'Hello' becomes a tool call with empty args.

3. **required as a security control.** The model must call `refund`; your executor still must refuse.

4. **Forgetting none after a dangerous failure.** The model retries the denied write.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which features set required versus none, and whether that is in code or only in a prompt. If everything is auto, ask them to name one feature that should not be. Confirm they do not treat required as auth.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- auto / required / none / forced-name are turn-level call policies.
- required means must call a tool, not may touch money.
- none stops side effects on draft or apology turns.
- Force a name when a router already picked the tool.
- Set the policy per feature; do not globalise auto.
- Log tool_choice so guessed prices can be diagnosed.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A price bot invents a fare on auto. What do you change? Set tool_choice to required or force get_price on that feature so a turn without a lookup is invalid. Still validate the result. Do not 'prompt harder' first. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When do you set none? Drafts, summaries, apologies after a denied write, and any turn where a tool would be a side-effect risk or a waste. Also when you already have the data and only need prose. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What do auto, required, and none mean for tool calling? auto lets the model call a tool or answer in text. required forces at least one tool call. none forbids tools this turn. A forced name requires that specific tool. None of these grant permission to execute. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

tool_choice is a per-turn policy: auto by default, required when the turn is worthless without a call, none when a call would be wrong, forced name when a router already decided. It is not authorisation.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: draw the tool loop** is a 90-second diagram: **model proposes**, **your code executes**, **you return a tool result**, **model finishes**. You label the second HTTP call, the call id, the cap, and the authorisation box inside execute. If you draw User → Model → Answer and hang a tool off the side, you missed the protocol.

This is M2.5's exam. They are testing whether you have implemented the loop, not whether you have used a decorator.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Almost every live-coding or design interview that mentions tools starts here. Candidates who say 'the model calls the API' fail. Candidates who draw the four hops, mention ids, and mention a cap pass — even if they forget a vendor flag name. On the job this diagram is also how you onboard the next engineer onto the executor.

## How it works + one small example

Talk while you box it:

1. User message.
2. Model → assistant tool_calls (id, name, args).
3. Your executor: validate, auth, run, cap.
4. Tool message(s) with those ids.
5. Model → user-visible text.
6. MAX steps around 2–5.

Say out loud: 'The model never holds the billing key. tool_choice can force a call; it cannot authorise one. I parse arguments only after the stream completes.' If they ask about parallel, you split reads and writes.

## Failure modes

1. **Stopping at execute.** You forgot the second model call.

2. **Model as executor.** Instant fail.

3. **No cap, no id.** You described a demo.

4. **No auth box.** You described a vulnerability.


## How you would defend it in a review

Time the drawing. If the second model call or the auth box is missing, they do not have the talking point. Ask a follow-up about two parallel get_order ids.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Whiteboard: propose, execute, result, second model call, answer.
- Label the call id, the cap, and the auth box.
- The model never executes the side effect.
- tool_choice is not authorisation.
- Mention parse-after-stream for arguments.
- A decorator-only story is not a loop.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You drew the loop but omitted ids and a cap. What will they ask? How parallel calls are paired and how you stop a cycle. Add call ids on the result messages and a MAX around the loop. Then show the change you would ship the same week. A candidate says the LLM calls refund via the SDK. How do you correct them? The SDK delivers a proposal. Our process runs refund after checks. The model only sees the result we append. If the SDK has an auto-executor, that executor is still our process. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What four hops must appear on a tool-loop whiteboard? Model proposes a tool call, your code executes (validate and auth), you return a tool result with the call id, the model is called again and produces the user-facing answer. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Model proposes, my code executes after validate and auth, I return a result with the call id, the model finishes. I cap the loop. That is the whole drawing.

names-descriptions-types.explain:
## What it is

A tool the model will pick is a **product interface**. The **name** should be a verb plus a noun (`create_refund`, not `helper2`). The **description** should say when to use it, when not to, and what each argument means, in language a stranger could implement from. The **types** should be the tightest schema you can defend: enums, patterns, required keys. **Error responses** should be short and structured so the model can recover (`not_found`, `denied`) instead of a stack trace.

Minimal parameters are a feature. Every extra argument is a chance to hallucinate and a chance to confuse. If you can bind a value from the session or from a previous result, do not ask the model for it.

This is industrial design for a reader that is a next-token predictor. Ambiguity in the spec becomes ambiguity in the call.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, most wrong tool calls are badly named twins or soggy descriptions. Interviewers will hand you a tool called `process` with a `data` string and ask you to rewrite it. They want a precise name, a when/when-not description, three typed fields, and an error object. They will ding `query: string` as a refused schema. This is also how you keep a new hire from implementing the wrong function.

## How it works + one small example

Rewrite this: `process(data: string) — does customer things`.

After: `get_order(order_id: ORD-\d+)` — 'Fetch one order the current user owns. Use when they name an id. Do not use to list orders or to refund.' Errors: `not_found`, `denied`. No `data`, no `user_id`.

Write the description first, then the function, then a unit test that the schema rejects `order_id=please`. Share the schema with the validator. Keep the blurb under a few hundred tokens unless an eval says more text lifts selection.

## Failure modes

1. **Cute or vague names.** `doIt`, `handle`, `api`. The model guesses.

2. **Essays as descriptions.** You blow the prompt and overlap with another tool.

3. **Untyped leftovers.** `meta: object` invites junk.

4. **Errors as HTML.** The model echoes internals or retries blindly.


## How you would defend it in a review

Hand the spec to someone who did not write the function. If they cannot implement it, the spec is not done. Ask which arguments are bound from the session. Ask to see the error object, not only the happy path.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Name = verb plus noun; description = when and when not.
- Tight types; minimal parameters; bind identity from the session.
- Structured error codes beat stack traces.
- A stranger should be able to implement the function from the spec.
- Extra arguments are extra hallucinations.
- Measure before lengthening descriptions.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The model keeps sending user_id. What should you change? Remove user_id from the schema and bind it in the executor from the session. Tell the description the tool is scoped to the current user. Do not 'prompt harder' to ignore the field. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Rewrite process(data: string) for fetching one order. get_order with required order_id (patterned), a description that forbids list and refund uses, and errors not_found/denied. Drop the catch-all data string. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What four qualities belong on a well-designed tool spec? A precise verb-noun name, a when/when-not description, a tight parameter schema with few fields, and useful structured error responses. Identity is bound from the session, not the spec. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I design tools as interfaces: a verb-noun name, a when/when-not description, tight types, and short error codes. I drop every argument I can bind myself.

ambiguous-overlapping-tools.explain:
## What it is

The model picks a tool by reading names and descriptions together. If two tools **overlap** — `search_orders` and `get_order` both described as 'find orders', or `refund` and `credit` with no difference — it will flip a coin. **Ambiguous** tools have vague verbs (`update`, `handle`) that match too many user sentences. Both failures look like 'the model is bad at tools'. Both are spec bugs.

Overlap is worse than a missing tool. A missing tool the model cannot call. Two twins it will call the wrong one with high confidence. The fix is to split jobs until a stranger can tell them apart in one sentence, or to merge twins into one tool with an enum.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, adding 'just one more helper' is how catalogues rot. Interviewers will show two overlapping specs and ask why selection is noisy. They want you to merge or to write a when-not line that is mutually exclusive. They will also ask how you detect overlap: an eval set of utterances labelled with the intended tool, not vibes.

## How it works + one small example

Put the catalogue on one page. For each pair, write a sentence only one of them satisfies.

Example. `get_order` = fetch exactly one id the user named. `search_orders` = list by date or status when no id is present. If the user says 'ORD-9', only the first is legal. Put that in both descriptions. If you cannot write those sentences, merge them into `lookup_order(mode: id|query, ...)`.

Run 50 utterances. If two tools split a cluster, you have overlap. Do not add a third tool to 'clarify'.

## Failure modes

1. **Twins with synonyms.** `fetch_order` and `get_order`. Delete one.

2. **When-not missing.** Each description is a marketing blurb.

3. **Fixing overlap with a longer system prompt** instead of changing the catalogue.

4. **No selection eval.** You discover twins in production.


## How you would defend it in a review

Spread the catalogue on the table. Ask for a when-not sentence per pair. If two tools share a synonym and no exclusive sentence, the PR adds overlap. Ask for the selection confusion matrix, even a small one.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Overlap and vague verbs look like model errors; they are spec bugs.
- Two twins are worse than one missing tool.
- Each pair needs a sentence only one tool satisfies.
- Merge twins or split jobs; do not add a third clarifier.
- Measure tool selection on labelled utterances.
- Do not patch overlap with a longer system prompt.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You have fetch_order and get_order. What do you do? Delete or merge one. Keep a single get_order with a tight schema. Two synonyms cannot be disambiguated by more prose. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you prove two tools do not overlap? Write a when-not sentence for each, then run a labelled utterance set and look at confusion pairs. If a cluster splits, merge or rewrite until one tool owns it. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why do overlapping tools cause wrong selections? The model matches names and descriptions. If two specs cover the same utterances, it samples between them. That looks like flakiness and is a catalogue design bug. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Overlapping tools make the model guess. I write mutually exclusive when/when-not lines, I merge twins, and I measure selection on labelled utterances.

too-many-undifferentiated-tools.explain:
## What it is

A catalogue of **dozens of near-identical tools** (or one tool with **fifteen optional arguments**) overwhelms the model's attention. Each spec is more prompt to read and more chance to pick wrong. 'Undifferentiated' means a human cannot tell them apart without tribal knowledge. Quantity without distinction is worse than a small, sharp set.

Unnecessary arguments are a second catalogue: `get_order(id, include_foo, include_bar, format, locale, debug, raw)` is five tools hiding in one, plus invitation to hallucinate flags. Prefer a small required core and server-side defaults.

There is no magic number, but if you cannot recite the catalogue from memory, the model probably cannot either.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, platforms grow a tool per microservice. Selection quality falls and nobody notices because each team added 'just one'. Interviewers will ask how many tools you attach. They want: as few as the turn needs, retrieved or routed if the platform is large, never the whole company dump. They will also ask you to delete arguments. This is a seniority tell.

## How it works + one small example

Budget the turn. A support bot might attach `get_order`, `get_policy`, `create_refund` — three. A platform with 80 APIs uses a **router** or **tool retrieval**: embed the user turn, attach the top 4 specs, not all 80.

Example. You inherited 22 tools. You cluster them, merge twins, drop unused (zero calls in 14 days), and retrieve the rest. Selection accuracy on a 100-utterance set jumps because the model is no longer reading a phone book.

For arguments, start with one required id. Add a flag only when an eval shows the model needs it and the server cannot default it.

## Failure modes

1. **Attach everything.** Prompt is 6k tokens of specs. TTFT dies and picks get worse.

2. **One mega-tool with twenty optionals.** The model fills three at random.

3. **Never deleting.** Dead tools still occupy attention.

4. **No router on a large platform.** You insist the model 'should be able to handle 80'.


## How you would defend it in a review

Count the tools on the turn and the optional fields on the widest one. If either number needs a spreadsheet, ask for a cut or a router. Ask when a tool was last deleted.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Too many similar tools make selection worse, not more capable.
- Retrieve or route when the platform catalogue is large.
- Drop unused tools; they still cost attention.
- Prefer a small required core over optional flag piles.
- If you cannot recite the catalogue, it is too big for the turn.
- One mega-tool with twenty optionals is a hidden catalogue.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A platform team wants every microservice exposed as a tool. What do you propose instead? A router or tool-retrieval step that attaches the top k specs for this utterance, plus a few always-on tools. Do not dump the company into the prompt. Then show the change you would ship the same week. A tool has twelve optional booleans. What do you do? Default them server-side and keep a small required core. Add a flag back only when an eval shows the model must choose it. Optionals are extra chances to hallucinate. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why does attaching 80 tools to every turn hurt? Each spec consumes prompt tokens and attention, and undifferentiated names confuse selection. TTFT also rises. Attach a small relevant set via a router or retrieval. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I attach the fewest distinct tools the turn needs, I delete twins and dead specs, and I refuse mega-argument lists. A large platform retrieves or routes tools; it does not dump the catalogue.

treating-arguments-as-untrusted.explain:
## What it is

Model-generated arguments are **untrusted input**. Schema-valid is not **business-valid**. You still check types (again), values (ranges, patterns), **permissions** (does this user own this id?), and **destructive** operations (refund, delete, email) with an extra gate: allow-list, confirm, or a human. The model is a stranger filling a form. You are the service that may submit it.

This is the same rule as a public HTTP API. If you would not take `{order_id, amount}` from an anonymous POST without checks, you do not take it from a tool call. Constrained decoding does not change that.

Log what you actually executed, not only what was proposed. After validation you may have coerced or rejected fields; the audit should show the executed view.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is the line that stops a prompt-injected ticket from refunding a stranger. Interviewers will ask whether you trust tool arguments. No is the start of the answer. Then: schema, ACL, destructive confirm, audit. They will ding 'the model is on our side'. They will also ask for an example where schema-valid still must fail (someone else's order id).

## How it works + one small example

Executor gates, in order:

1. Parse + schema.
2. Normalise (trim, uppercase prefix).
3. ACL: resource belongs to session user.
4. Business predicates (amount ≤ remaining, status in refundable).
5. Destructive: extra confirm or allow-listed reason code.
6. Execute with idempotency key.
7. Audit executed args.

Example. Args `{order_id: ORD-9, amount: 999999}` parse. ACL passes if ORD-9 is theirs. Predicate `amount ≤ remaining` fails. You return `invalid_amount` and never call billing. A second example: ORD-9 is not theirs. You return `denied` without confirming the order exists, if that is your policy.

## Failure modes

1. **Schema-only.** Wrong-owner ids sail through.

2. **No extra gate on delete/refund/email.** One injected sentence moves money.

3. **Auditing the proposal, not the executed args.** You cannot replay what happened.

4. **Coercing silently.** You chopped a huge amount to max and refunded without telling anyone.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask where ACL runs relative to the billing call. If it is missing, reject. Ask what a refund requires besides a valid schema. Ask to see an audit row for a denied call.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Schema-valid is not business-valid or authorised.
- Check ACL and predicates before the downstream call.
- Destructive tools need an extra gate (confirm, allow-list).
- Audit executed arguments, not only the proposal.
- Do not silently coerce money or ids.
- Treat the model like an anonymous HTTP client.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. ORD-9 belongs to someone else but parses. What does the executor return? denied (and, depending on policy, without confirming the order exists). It does not call billing. This is an ACL fail, not a schema fail. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What extra gate do you put on refund or send_email? An allow-listed reason code, an authenticated confirm that the model cannot mint, or a human approval. Plus an idempotency key. A valid schema is not enough. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why is a schema-valid tool call still untrusted? The model can put another user's id, an out-of-range amount, or a destructive action the user did not want. Schema checks shape. You still check ACL, predicates, and extra gates. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Tool arguments are untrusted. I validate types, values, permissions, and destructive ops before any side effect, and I audit what I actually executed.

Treat the model like an anonymous HTTP client.

questions.q: Why is a schema-valid tool call still untrusted?
questions.a: The model can put another user's id, an out-of-range amount, or a destructive action the user did not want. Schema checks shape. You still check ACL, predicates, and extra gates.

questions.q: ORD-9 belongs to someone else but parses. What does the executor return?
questions.a: denied (and, depending on policy, without confirming the order exists). It does not call billing. This is an ACL fail, not a schema fail.

questions.q: What extra gate do you put on refund or send_email?
questions.a: An allow-listed reason code, an authenticated confirm that the model cannot mint, or a human approval. Plus an idempotency key. A valid schema is not enough.

questions.q: What belongs in the audit row?
questions.a: The executed arguments after validation, the actor (session user), the tool-call id, and the outcome. Not only the raw proposal, and not the downstream secret.

questions.q: A teammate clamps amount to the remaining balance and proceeds. Why is that risky?
questions.a: Silent coercion hides a model or user error and can refund the wrong figure. Reject invalid_amount or require confirm. Do not quietly change money.

tool-descriptions-are-context.explain:
## What it is

Tool **descriptions sit in the prompt**. They are not comments for humans only. The model uses that text, plus names and schemas, to decide **whether** to call and **how** to fill arguments. A vague blurb is a vague policy. A contradictory blurb ('use for refunds' on a read-only fetch) is a landmine. A 2_000-token essay is a tax on every turn, including turns that never call the tool.

Because descriptions are context, they are also an injection surface if you generate them from user content or from an untrusted catalogue. Keep them static, reviewed, and boring. They are also a cache-busting surface: if you interpolate today's date into a description, the prefix cache dies.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people edit descriptions like README files and do not realise they changed production policy. Interviewers will ask what the model sees besides the user sentence. The tool list is the answer. They want you to treat description edits as prompt changes: version them, eval selection, and do not generate them from tickets. This is the same hygiene as system-prompt edits.

## How it works + one small example

Store descriptions in versioned files next to the schema. Review them like copy that ships. Example: you add 'Do not use when the user only says thanks' to `create_refund` after an eval showed false positives. You ship it as a prompt version, not a drive-by string change.

Do not build descriptions with `{user.notes}`. Do not put secrets in them ('internal endpoint https://…'). Do not change them per request if you want a cacheable prefix — put per-request facts in the user message instead.

When selection is wrong, read the descriptions the model actually received, not the ones in last week's wiki.

## Failure modes

1. **Drive-by edits** with no eval and no version.

2. **User text inside the description.** Injection and cache busts.

3. **Secrets or internal URLs** in the blurb. They can be echoed.

4. **Descriptions that contradict the schema** (says optional, schema says required).


## How you would defend it in a review

Diff the description like a prompt. Ask for a selection eval if it changed. Grep for interpolation and URLs. If today's date is in the catalogue, ask why the prefix must miss.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Tool descriptions are context the model reads every turn.
- Edit them like prompts: version, review, eval selection.
- Do not generate descriptions from user content.
- Do not put secrets or volatile clocks in the catalogue.
- Contradiction between blurb and schema causes bad fills.
- Long blurbs tax TTFT even on turns that call nothing.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A PM pastes a customer email into a tool description to 'explain the case'. What is wrong? User text in the catalogue is untrusted, busts the prefix cache, and can inject instructions. Put the email in the user message, fenced. Keep descriptions static. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you ship a description change safely? Version it like a prompt, run the tool-selection eval, and watch false-positive calls. Do not hot-edit a string in a running process without a pin. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why are tool descriptions part of the context window? Providers send the catalogue with the request. The model attends to names, blurbs, and schemas when choosing a tool. They cost tokens on every turn, not only when a tool is called. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Descriptions are prompt tokens. I version them, I keep them static and reviewed, I never interpolate user text into them, and I treat an edit as a prompt change that needs a selection eval.

questions.a: It busts prompt caching and rarely improves selection. Put 'as of' timestamps in the user turn or a small facts block instead.
