questions.a: The model omits amount; your validator fails; repair rate climbs. Align the sentences with the schema. The description is not decoration.

one-tool-one-job.explain:
## What it is

**One tool, one job** is how you stop the model guessing between twins. A job is one side effect or one fetch the user can name in a sentence: fetch this order, create this refund, search the policy corpus. If you need two jobs, you want two tools or a workflow, not a Swiss-army `manage_order(action, ...)`.

Twins appear when two tools share a verb or a noun and neither description excludes the other. The model then samples. Splitting is not the same as exploding into 80 micro-tools: you split until jobs are exclusive, then you stop. Merge if two tools are the same job with synonyms.

This is the design rule behind the overlap note. Say it in interviews as a slogan you can implement.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, `manage_*` tools become untestable and over-authorised. Interviewers will ask you to split a fat tool. They want two names, two schemas, two auth policies (read vs write), and a when-not line. They will also stop you if you split into nonsense (`get_order_status`, `get_order_total`, `get_order_items`) that should be one fetch.

## How it works + one small example

Take `manage_order(action: get|refund|cancel, id, amount?)`. Split:

- `get_order(order_id)` read, any support agent.
- `create_refund(order_id, amount)` write, extra gate.
- `cancel_order(order_id)` write, extra gate.

The model can still call them in sequence. Auth is no longer one mega-permission. Descriptions are exclusive: get does not mention money.

Do **not** split `get_order` into three field getters unless an eval shows the payload is too large. That is the other failure mode: too many undifferentiated shards.

## Failure modes

1. **Fat action enums.** One permission to rule them all.

2. **Synonym twins** after a split (`fetch` and `get`).

3. **Sharding a read into twelve getters** the model cannot choose among.

4. **A workflow stuffed into one tool** with a JSON blob argument.


## How you would defend it in a review

If you see action: enum with write verbs beside reads, ask for a split. If you see twelve getters for one resource, ask for a merge. The test is whether a stranger can pick the name from a user sentence.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- One side effect or one fetch per tool.
- Split fat action enums so auth can differ.
- Stop splitting once jobs are exclusive; do not shard a read to death.
- Merge synonym twins after a split.
- A workflow is a loop of tools, not one blob argument.
- Read versus write is the first split that pays off.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. When is splitting a get_order into field getters a mistake? When the model must pick among near-identical reads and the payload was fine as one object. That creates undifferentiated twins. Split only if size or auth requires it. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Split manage_order(action: get|refund|cancel). get_order as a read, create_refund and cancel_order as separate writes with extra gates. The model may call them in sequence. Do not keep one mega-permission. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What does one tool, one job mean in practice? Each tool has one fetch or one side effect a user can name, exclusive when-not text, and its own auth. Fat action enums and synonym twins both violate it. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

One tool, one job: exclusive names and auth. I split fat action enums into read versus write, and I stop splitting once a stranger can tell them apart.

questions.a: No. Use the loop: get_order then create_refund. The workflow lives in your cap and your UI confirm, not in a blob argument.

argument-validation-before-side-effects.explain:
## What it is

**Schema-valid is not business-valid.** Before any side effect you check **ids** (format and existence), **units** (cents versus dollars, timezones, currencies), **ranges**, and **state** (is this order refundable *now*?). The schema can say `amount: number`. Business-valid says `0 < amount ≤ remaining` in the currency of the order, not the model's favourite currency.

This check lives in the executor, in code you test, not in the description. Descriptions help the model propose; they do not protect the ledger. If a check can be written as a predicate, write it. If it needs a human, stop and ask.

Do the checks **before** the HTTP call that moves money or sends mail. After is an incident report.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, unit bugs (dollars sent as cents) are more common than cartoon prompt injections. Interviewers will ask for an example where JSON Schema passed and you still refused. Amount vs remaining, id ownership, and 'already cancelled' are the trio. They want the predicate in code, plus a test. This is the sibling of M2.4's syntactic vs semantic split, applied to tools.

## How it works + one small example

For `create_refund`:

1. Schema: order_id pattern, amount number, currency enum.
2. Load order (ACL).
3. Units: if the model sent dollars and the ledger is cents, convert in one obvious place or reject — do not guess.
4. `amount <= remaining` and status in `{paid, fulfilled}`.
5. Then billing, with an idempotency key.

Example. `{order_id: ORD-9, amount: 14, currency: USD}` parses. Remaining is 1400 cents. If you treat 14 as cents you under-refund; as dollars you match. The spec must say the unit, the validator must enforce it, and the test must use 14 with an expected 1400 cents or a reject.

Never 'fix' units silently in production without a log.

## Failure modes

1. **Trusting the number type.** -2 and 1e12 both parse.

2. **Guessing cents vs dollars.** You will be wrong half the year.

3. **Checking state after the charge.** You cannot unsend easily.

4. **Putting the predicate only in the description.** The model will still miss it.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for the unit test that 14 dollars is not 14 cents. Ask where live status is loaded. If predicates exist only in the description, the review fails.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Business predicates run after schema and before the side effect.
- Ids, units, ranges, and live state are the usual checks.
- Write units in the spec and enforce them; do not guess cents.
- Descriptions cannot protect a ledger.
- Test predicates with real amounts and statuses.
- Do not silently convert money without a log.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The spec forgot to say cents versus dollars. What do you do in the executor? Refuse to guess. Pin the unit in the schema (enum or a field name like amount_cents), add a test, and reject ambiguous payloads until that ships. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Where should 'order must be refundable now' live? In executor code that loads current state, plus a test. Not only in the tool description. State changes; a blurb does not re-check. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Give an example of schema-valid, business-invalid tool args. amount: 999999 against a $14 remaining balance, or order_id that exists but is cancelled, or a currency that is not the order's. All parse; all must fail before billing. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Schema-valid is not business-valid. I check ids, units, ranges, and live state in code before any side effect, and I test those predicates with real numbers.

questions.a: No. You need a unit, a range against remaining, and usually a currency that matches the order. number only means it parsed as numeric.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: rewrite a bad tool spec** is a live edit. They will give you `helper(data: string) — does stuff` or `manage_order(action, payload)`. You tighten the **name**, the **description**, and the **types** until a stranger could implement the function and a model could pick it. You add when-not text, you bind identity from the session, you split writes from reads, and you name the error codes.

This is M2.6 in one exercise. Talking about 'good tools' without rewriting the spec is a fail.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is a favourite whiteboard because it shows product sense, security, and prompting in ten minutes. Interviewers listen for exclusive jobs, tight types, no user_id argument, and an extra gate on writes. They do not need vendor flag names. On the job this is also how you review a PR that added a tool.

## How it works + one small example

Work out loud:

1. Rename to a verb-noun.
2. Write when / when-not in two sentences.
3. Replace `data` with two or three typed fields; drop user_id.
4. Mark read vs write; add errors `not_found`, `denied`.
5. Say what you validate before the side effect (ACL, units).

Example start: `process(data)`. End: `get_order(order_id)` plus, if needed, `create_refund(order_id, amount_cents)`. Close with: 'I would eval selection on 50 utterances before shipping the split.'

## Failure modes

1. **Only adding adjectives** to the old description.

2. **Keeping the fat action enum** because it felt convenient.

3. **Forgetting ACL and units** in the spoken rewrite.

4. **Inventing twelve micro-tools** to look thorough.


## How you would defend it in a review

Give them helper(data) and time the rewrite. If the result still has a catch-all string or a user_id argument, they do not have the talking point. Listen for ACL and units.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Live-edit name, description, and types — do not add adjectives.
- A stranger must be able to implement the function from the spec.
- Split fat enums; bind user_id from the session.
- Mention ACL, units, and error codes in the rewrite.
- Stop at exclusive jobs; do not shard into twelve getters.
- Promise a small selection eval, not a vibe.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A candidate adds please be careful to the old helper description. Why is that a fail? Adjectives do not change the interface. The name, types, and job boundaries are still mush. Interviewers want a spec a stranger could implement. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Rewrite manage_order(action, payload) on the whiteboard. Split into get_order(order_id) and create_refund(order_id, amount_cents). Bind user from the session. Write exclusive when-not lines. Add not_found/denied. Mention ACL and remaining-balance checks. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What three parts of a bad tool spec do you rewrite first? The name (verb plus noun), the description (when and when-not), and the parameter types (drop catch-all strings, add required ids and units). Then auth and errors. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I rewrite the name, the when/when-not, and the types until a stranger could implement it. I split writes from reads, I bind identity myself, and I say what I validate before the side effect.

beyond-prompt-model-answer.explain:
## What it is

Most useful features are not **prompt → model → answer**. They are **workflows**: several LLM calls, tool calls, deterministic transforms, and application logic stitched with your control flow. Examples: extract then classify; retrieve then generate; route by intent then run a specialist; fan out summaries and merge. The model is a step. The workflow is the product.

Thinking only in single prompts produces god-prompts that try to do five jobs, fail silently, and cannot be tested. Thinking in workflows lets you pin, eval, and retry each step. It also lets you put non-model steps where they belong: regex, DB lookups, ACL, price tables.

This module is about owning that graph before anyone says 'agent'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the first production feature that works is usually a two-step workflow, not a clever prompt. Interviewers will ask you to break a messy task into calls. They want named steps, a contract between them, and a reason each step is a model versus code. They will ding a single 2_000-token prompt that 'does everything'. This is the design skill that separates Level 2 from Level 1.

## How it works + one small example

Write the steps on a pad before you write prompts.

Example. 'Summarise this ticket and file it.' Step 1: extract `{product, urgency, quote}` (schema). Step 2: code maps urgency to a queue. Step 3: a second, cheaper model drafts the summary from the quote only. Step 4: your code inserts the row. One god-prompt that also files the row is how you get a well-written summary in the wrong queue.

Each model step has its own schema, timeout, and eval slice. The workflow has a trace id.

## Failure modes

1. **God-prompt.** Five jobs, one call, no tests.

2. **Model where code would do.** Asking the LLM to add two numbers or to look up a price you have in a table.

3. **No contract between steps.** Step 2 cannot parse step 1.

4. **Calling it an agent** because there are two calls. It is still your graph.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to draw the steps before the prompts. If there is one box, push for a split. Ask which steps are code. Ask where the trace id sits.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- A feature is often several calls plus code, not one prompt.
- Name steps and give each a contract you can test.
- Use code for lookups, ACL, and arithmetic.
- A trace id covers the whole workflow.
- Two calls do not make an agent if you own the graph.
- God-prompts hide failures and block evals.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Step 2 cannot parse step 1's output. What was missing? A schema contract and validation between steps. The workflow should fail closed at the boundary, not hope the next prompt understands a paragraph. Then show the change you would ship the same week. A teammate writes one prompt that extracts, classifies, and files a ticket. What do you change? Split extract (schema), classify or map in code, draft with a second call if needed, file in code. Eval each step. Do not let the model write the database row from a paragraph. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is a workflow in this module, versus a single prompt? A graph you own: multiple LLM calls, tools, and deterministic steps with contracts between them. A single prompt is one node. Most products need the graph. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I design features as workflows: named steps, some model, some code, with a contract between them. I refuse one enormous prompt that tries to be the product.

questions.a: You still own the edges: which step runs next is in your code. An agent would choose the next step itself. That is a later, costlier pattern.

sequential-routed-fan-out-patterns.explain:
## What it is

Three orchestration patterns cover most of Level 2. **Sequential**: A then B, B sees A's output (extract then draft). **Routed**: an if/else or a cheap classifier picks one specialist path (billing vs bug). **Fan-out / fan-in**: run several independent calls, then **join** (summarise three docs, merge). These are application-controlled. You write the edges.

Routing can be code (keyword, rule) or a small model. Fan-out needs a join that defines what happens if one arm is empty or failed. Sequential needs a contract at each hop. None of these require an agent loop.

Learn to name the pattern in a design review. 'We will use a chain' is not a pattern.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, picking the wrong pattern is how you either serialise independent work (slow) or parallelise a dependency (wrong). Interviewers will describe a product and ask which pattern. They want the name, a sketch, and the failure policy on the join. They will ding an agent proposal for a stable if/else.

## How it works + one small example

Map the task.

- Ticket → extract → draft: sequential.
- User sentence → billing or tech path: routed (start with rules; add a model if rules fail an eval).
- Three policies → three summaries → merge: fan-out, then a merge prompt or a deterministic concat with a cap.

Example join: if one of three retrieves is empty, merge the two and flag `partial=true`. Do not invent the third. If the router is unsure, take a default path or ask a clarifying question — do not run all specialists 'just in case' without a budget.

## Failure modes

1. **Fan-out without a join policy.** One 500 kills the user turn, or you drop successes.

2. **Router that is a 70B agent.** You needed an if.

3. **Sequential when arms are independent.** You gift 2× latency.

4. **Calling every pattern a pipeline.** You cannot debug what you cannot name.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to label the boxes sequential, routed, or fan-out. Ask the join policy in the same breath. If they say agent for a two-way if, send them back to a routing table.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Sequential, routed, and fan-out/fan-in cover most Level 2 graphs.

when-to-split-a-task.explain:
## What it is

Split a task when **one prompt is doing two jobs that fail independently**, when **outputs need different schemas**, when **one part is code**, or when **context for A drowns B**. Do not split when the jobs share so much state that the second call would need to resend everything, or when you have not measured a failure. Splitting is a response to a named problem, not a virtue.

A useful test: can you write an eval for step 1 that does not care about step 2? If yes, you have a seam. Another test: does step 2 need a smaller, cleaner input than the raw user blob? Then extract first.

Avoid splitting into a dozen micro-calls that each add TTFT and a new timeout. Two or three steps is the usual win.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the god-prompt is how teams hide a 20% extract error behind a fluent summary. Interviewers will give you a fat prompt and ask where you cut. They want a seam, a schema, and a reason — not 'we always chunk work'. They will also stop you from proposing an eight-step chain for a greeting.

## How it works + one small example

Start with one call and an eval. If extract labels are wrong but tone is fine, split extract (tight schema) from draft (style). If the model loses the question under a 4k policy, retrieve or extract the clause first, then answer.

Example. 'Read the PDF and file a Jira ticket.' Split: extract `{title, repro, expected}` from a page-limited excerpt (model), validate (code), create Jira (code). Asking one prompt to 'be the ticket' dumps prose into Jira and skips fields.

Do not split 'say hello' into classify-intent plus greet. Measure first.

## Failure modes

1. **Splitting for fashion.** Eight calls, same quality, 4× latency.

2. **No seam.** The second call needs the entire raw blob anyway.

3. **Splitting and then not validating** the first schema.

4. **Never splitting a god-prompt** that has two KPIs.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which KPI failed and whether that step can be scored alone. If they split without a seam or an eval, the graph is fashion. If they refuse to split a two-KPI god-prompt, push the other way.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Split when jobs fail independently or need different contracts.
- A seam is a step you can eval without the next step.
- Do not split until you have a named failure or a code step.
- Two or three steps beat a twelve-call graph for most tasks.
- God-prompts hide the worse KPI behind fluent text.
- If step 2 still needs the whole blob, you did not find a seam.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A god-prompt files fluent tickets with the wrong priority 20% of the time. Where do you cut? Extract {priority, ...} under a schema and eval that slice, then draft. Priority is a KPI that the fluent prose was hiding. Map priority in code if it is a table. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why is an eval that only scores the final paragraph a reason to split? It cannot see which job failed. After a split you can score extract and draft separately and stop fixing the wrong step. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: When should you split a task into multiple LLM calls? When two jobs fail independently, need different schemas, or one part should be code, or when context for A drowns B. Not as a default, and not into a dozen micro-calls. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I split when two jobs fail independently or need different schemas, I keep the graph small, and I do not split as a fashion. A seam is a step I can eval alone.

building-by-hand-then-composing.explain:
## What it is

Build the workflow **by hand first**: functions, ifs, explicit `complete()` calls, printed messages. Then, if the graph is stable and the glue is repetitive, **reproduce it** with LangChain composition (or another runner). Hand-built is how you learn the control flow and the failure paths. Composition is how you stop copy-pasting once you understand them.

Reversing the order — starting from a clever LCEL graph — is how you ship a pipe you cannot step through. The composition should be a refactor of a flow you already tested, not an exploration environment.

This is the same advice as raw-SDK-then-LangChain, applied to multi-step graphs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, inherited LCEL that nobody can draw is a tax. Interviewers will ask you to implement a router without a framework, then say how you would wrap it. They want the if/else in your language, then an optional pipe. A candidate who can only write `RunnableBranch` without explaining the cases has not built the flow.

## How it works + one small example

Day one: `def handle(ticket):` with extract(), route(), draft(), file(), tests for each. Day two: if you will grow more specialists, wrap extract|draft as named runnables and keep `route()` as a function you can read.

Example. You hand-build fan-out of three retrieves and a merge. You discover the join policy (partial ok). Only then do you write a `RunnableParallel` plus a merge prompt. The join policy stays in your code, not in a lambda you cannot name.

If composition fights you for more than an hour, keep the functions. Clarity wins.

## Failure modes

1. **Framework-first.** You cannot draw the graph without the docs.

2. **Composition that hides the join policy** in an anonymous lambda.

3. **Never refactoring** five copy-pasted complete() calls that are now identical.

4. **Tests only on the composed object** so you cannot run a step.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to draw the function version. If they can only paste LCEL, the graph is not theirs. Ask where the join policy lives after the refactor.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Hand-build the graph before you pipe it.
- Composition should reproduce a flow you can already draw.
- Keep join and route policies in named functions.
- If the framework fights you, keep the functions.
- Test steps independently, not only the composed object.
- Copy-pasted complete() calls are a later refactor, not a sin on day one.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You cannot explain what a RunnableBranch does in your app. What should you do? Rewrite the cases as a function you can read, add tests, then wrap if you still want the pipe. Do not debug via library folklore. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What belongs in a function even after you compose? Routing tables, join policies, ACL, and any if that a new hire must find in a minute. Do not hide those in anonymous lambdas. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why build a workflow by hand before using LCEL or similar? So you understand control flow, contracts, and failure paths. The pipe should refactor a tested graph, not invent one you cannot step through. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I build the workflow with functions and ifs first, I test the seams, then I compose if the glue is repetitive. Composition is a refactor, not a starting point.

workflows-vs-agents.explain:
## What it is

A **workflow** is a graph **you** wrote: the next step is an if, a sequence, or a join you can test. An **agent** is a loop where the **model chooses** the next tool or step, often until it says it is done. Both use LLMs and tools. They differ in who owns the edges. Workflows are cheaper to eval, cheaper to cap, and easier to explain in an incident. Agents are for tasks whose path you cannot write down in advance.

Level 2 wants you to prefer workflows. Agents arrive later (and still need caps, auth, and traces). Calling a two-step extract-then-draft an agent is a category error that hides how simple the product is.

A useful sentence: if you can draw the graph on a card, it is a workflow. If the card would say 'then it figures it out', you are proposing an agent — and you need a reason.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, 'let's make it an agent' is how a stable refund path becomes an unbounded loop. Interviewers will ask when you refuse an agent. The answer is this note plus the interview talking point at the end of the module. They want: known graph → workflow; unknown, long-horizon, tool-heavy exploration → consider an agent, with a cap. They will ding agent-as-default.

## How it works + one small example

Refund path: get order → confirm → refund. That is a workflow, even if each step uses a model. Research path: 'find anything about this incident in six systems' with a tool set that depends on what you find — that may be an agent, with MAX steps and a write-lock.

Example. A PM says 'agentic support'. You draw the five intents you already have. They fit a router. You ship a workflow. You revisit an agent only if an eval shows a long tail of intents you cannot list.

Write the refusal down: 'stable, short, known graph stays a workflow'.

## Failure modes

1. **Agent as a synonym for 'uses tools'.** Every tool loop becomes unbounded.

2. **Workflow that secretly loops** without a cap (you built an agent by accident).

3. **Agent without a write-lock.** It refunds while exploring.

4. **No reason for the agent** except a blog post.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask who chooses the next step. If they say the model and the graph is three boxes, refuse the agent. Ask for the cap and the write-lock if they still want a loop.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Workflow: you own the next step. Agent: the model chooses it.
- Prefer workflows when the graph is known and short.
- Using tools does not make a system an agent.
- An uncapped loop is an accidental agent.
- Agents need a reason, a cap, and write locks.
- Refuse 'agentic' as a synonym for a router.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Your 'workflow' calls complete() in a while True until the model says done. What is it? An agent, and a reckless one: no cap. Add MAX, or better, write the real graph if you know it. Then show the change you would ship the same week. A PM wants an agentic refund. The path is get → confirm → refund. What do you ship? A workflow. The graph is known and short. An agent adds an unbounded loop and a write risk for no eval gain. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is the difference between a workflow and an agent? In a workflow your code chooses the next step. In an agent the model chooses, usually in a loop. Both may use tools. Ownership of the edges is the split. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

If I can draw the graph, it is a workflow and I own the edges. I refuse an agent for stable, short, known paths. Agents need a reason, a cap, and a lock on writes.

routing-tables-vs-an-agent.explain:
## What it is

A **routing table** is a documented map from intent (or a cheap signal) to a path: if `billing` then billing specialist; if `how-to` then docs RAG; else `other`. It can be rules, a small classifier, or both. It is **testable**: you can list cases and expected paths. A **free loop** (agent) that 'just figures out which tool to use' is harder to test, harder to cap, and harder to explain when it picks `refund` on a how-to question.

Start with the table. Promote a cell to a model classifier if rules miss a measured slice. Promote the whole thing to an agent only if the table cannot be written. Most support and internal-ops products never leave the table.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, routing tables are how you sleep. Interviewers will ask how you send a ticket to the right skill. They want a table, an eval, and a default cell — not an agent that browses tools. This is the 'refuse an agent' talking point in concrete form.

## How it works + one small example

Write the table in the repo: intent → path → owner → eval file. Example rows: `billing → get_order + policy`, `bug → create_ticket`, `other → clarify`. A keyword pass plus a small model on the remainder is enough for many desks.

When a new intent appears, add a row. If rows explode and overlap, you have an M2.6 catalogue problem, not an agent-shaped problem. Agents do not fix overlapping intents; they hide them.

## Failure modes

1. **Agent as the first router.** You cannot list what it should have done.

2. **Table in a slide, not in the repo.** The code is still a loop.

3. **No default cell.** Unknown intents fall into a write path.

4. **Overlapping rows** with no owner. Two specialists fire.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see the table in the repo and the default cell. If routing is 'the agent decides', ask for last week's traces grouped by intended path. No table is a reject for a stable product.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- A routing table maps intent to a path you can test.
- Rules first, small classifier second, agent last.
- Unknown intents need a default cell, not a write.
- Overlapping rows are a catalogue bug, not an agent need.
- The table lives in the repo next to its eval file.
- Agents hide overlapping intents; they do not fix them.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The 'router' is an agent with twelve tools and no table. What is the bug? You cannot say what should have happened. Extract the intents you already see into a table, measure, and shrink the loop. The agent was hiding the design. Then show the change you would ship the same week. A new intent appears weekly. Do you switch to an agent? First add a row and an eval case. If rows overlap or explode, clean the catalogue. Consider an agent only if you truly cannot list the paths. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why is a routing table easier to test than an agent loop? Each intent has an expected path you can assert. An agent has a tree of tool traces you must judge after the fact. Tables fail closed on unknown rows; loops wander. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A documented if/else over intent is easier to test than a free loop. I ship a routing table with a default cell, and I only add a model or an agent when the table cannot cover a measured slice.

fan-out-then-merge.explain:
## What it is

**Fan-out** runs independent work in parallel. **Merge** (fan-in) waits and combines. The easy part is `gather`. The hard part is the **join policy**: what if one arm is empty, slow, or failed? What is the merged schema? How do you cap tokens so three summaries do not blow the next prompt? A join that assumes all arms are 200 OK is a production bug.

Merges can be deterministic (concat with headings and a size cap) or a small model call (synthesise). Deterministic is easier to test. Use a model merge when you need conflict resolution or de-duplication you cannot write as code.

Always attach the source id to each arm so the merge can cite or drop.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, fan-out is how you keep p95 tolerable; bad joins are how you ship partial lies. Interviewers will ask what happens if one retrieve returns nothing. They want a policy: drop and flag, fail the turn, or retry that arm once — written down. They will ding `Promise.all` with no empty-arm story.

## How it works + one small example

Define `JoinResult {parts: [...], missing: [...], failed: [...]}`. Example: three docs. Arm 2 empty, arm 3 500. You merge 1 with `partial=true`, you do not invent 2, you may retry 3 once, you tell the next step which sources exist.

Token cap: each arm summary ≤ 400 tokens, merge prompt ≤ 1_200. Overflow drops the lowest-scoring arm, logged.

Timeout: a slow arm after T ms becomes `failed` so the user is not held hostage by one retrieve.

## Failure modes

1. **All-or-nothing join.** One 500 hides two good arms.

2. **Silent drop.** You merge two and never flag partial.

3. **Unbounded concat.** The next call 400s on context.

4. **Model merge that invents the missing arm** to sound complete.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for the join policy in writing: empty, failed, timeout, token cap. If they only show gather, the review is incomplete. Ask whether a model merge is allowed to mention a missing source.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- gather is easy; the join policy is the product.
- Define empty, failed, and slow arms before you code.
- Flag partial merges; do not invent missing branches.
- Cap per-arm and merged tokens.
- Time out stragglers so one retrieve cannot hold the turn.
- Keep source ids on every arm.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Two of three retrieves succeed. The merge writes a fluent answer as if all three existed. What failed? The join invented or ignored missing. Return the two parts with partial=true and let the next step abstain on questions that needed the third source. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you stop a slow arm from owning p95? Per-arm timeout; promote the straggler to failed and merge the rest, or fail the turn if that arm was required. Do not wait forever. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What must a fan-in join specify besides waiting for all arms? What to do when an arm is empty, failed, or late; the merged schema; a token cap; and whether the result is marked partial. Waiting is the easy part. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Fan-out needs a join that names empty and failed arms, caps tokens, and times out stragglers. I never invent a missing branch to look complete.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: when you refuse an agent** is a one-minute stance: **stable, short workflows with a known graph stay as workflows**. You draw the boxes, you name sequential/routed/fan-out, you point at the routing table, and you say you would only open a free loop if you cannot write the edges — and then with a cap and a write-lock.

This is M2.7's exam. They are not asking you to hate agents. They are asking whether you reach for a loop before a table.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is a trending interview question because blogs oversold agents. Hiring managers want someone who will not turn a refund path into a research assistant. On the job this stance also saves you from a quarter of unnecessary agent infra.

## How it works + one small example

Say this:

1. 'If I can draw it, I ship a workflow.'
2. Sketch the graph (router + two specialists, or get-confirm-refund).
3. 'An agent is a model-chosen next step. I need a reason I cannot write the edges.'
4. 'If we still want a loop: MAX steps, no writes without a lock, eval against this workflow baseline.'

Close with the routing-table line: a documented if/else is easier to test than a free loop.

1. **Agent as default** because the job description said agentic.

2. **No graph** on the whiteboard — only a loop icon.

3. **Refusing agents forever** instead of giving the condition.

4. **Forgetting the cap** when you do allow a loop.


## How you would defend it in a review

Time the stance. They must draw a graph and say refuse. A candidate who only says agents are hype, or who agrees to an agent for a refund path, does not have the talking point.

That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Those stay workflows with a routing table. Agents need a reason the edges cannot be written. If the graph is known and short, I refuse an agent and ship a workflow. I use a routing table, I name the pattern, and I only open a loop with a cap and a write-lock when I cannot write the edges.

when-concurrency-helps.explain:
## What it is

A **synchronous** call waits for one completion before you start the next. An **asynchronous** call lets the worker do other work (or start more calls) while it waits on the network. **Concurrency** is running several of those waits at once. It helps when the bottleneck is **waiting** — many independent LLM requests, each idle on the vendor. It does not help when the bottleneck is **your CPU**, a **shared lock**, or a **rate limit you already saturate** with one in-flight call.

Concurrency is not parallelism of the model's decode. Each request still generates at its own tokens-per-second. You are overlapping waits. Throughput (requests per minute) can rise; per-request latency usually does not fall, and can rise if you overload the vendor or yourself.

User-facing turns with one call do not get faster because you imported asyncio. Fan-out of independent arms does.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, people `async` a single chat turn and wonder why p95 is unchanged. Interviewers will ask when concurrency helps. They want: many independent requests, wait-bound, with a bound so you do not 429. They will ding 'we made it async so it is faster' on a one-call path. This is also how you explain why a batch of evals should be concurrent and a checkout chat should not start eight extra calls.

## How it works + one small example

Draw a timeline.

- 10 independent classifications, 2s each, sequential: 20s. Concurrent with 5 in flight: ~4s plus jitter.
- 1 user chat, 2s: still 2s if you only have one call.

Measure: if CPU is low and you are waiting on HTTP, concurrency can help. If you are already at the vendor's RPM, you will trade 429s for 'throughput'. Put a semaphore first (next notes).

Do not confuse asyncio in the server with the vendor's async. Your worker can be async and still send one request.

## Failure modes

1. **Async as a speed spell** on a single turn.

2. **Unbounded create_task** for every user. You DDoS yourself and the vendor.

3. **Concurrent dependent steps.** B needs A; you raced them.

4. **Ignoring that p95 per request can worsen** under load.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask whether the work is independent and wait-bound. If they async a single call for speed, correct them. Ask what bound they will put on in-flight requests before they ship gather.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Concurrency overlaps I/O waits; it does not speed one decode.
- It helps many independent requests, not a single chat turn.
- Throughput can rise; per-request p95 can worsen if you overload.
- Dependent steps stay sequential.
- Async in your process is not the same as many in-flight vendor calls.
- Bound it or you will 429.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A team 'made the handler async' and p95 is unchanged. Why? The turn still has one vendor call. Async let the worker serve others, but this user's wait is the same. Concurrency helps a fan-out or a batch, not a single call. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Ten independent classifications, 2s each. Sequential vs five in flight? Sequential about 20s wall time. Five in flight about 4s plus jitter, if the vendor accepts that rate. Per-item latency stays ~2s. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: When does concurrency improve LLM throughput? When you have many independent, wait-bound requests and spare rate-limit budget. It overlaps HTTP waits. It does not shorten one model's decode. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Concurrency overlaps waits on independent requests. It raises throughput, not magic per-call speed. I use it when I am wait-bound and I can bound in-flight work.

Bound it or you will 429.

running-requests-concurrently.explain:
## What it is

To process **many independent** LLM requests you start several calls and wait for them as a group: `asyncio.gather`, a thread pool, a vendor batch helper, or LangChain `batch`/`abatch`. The unit of independence is 'B does not need A's output'. Eval sets, fan-out retrieves, and offline classification are the usual wins. User turns that must stay sequential stay sequential.

You still attach a timeout per call and a **bound** on how many are in flight (next note). A naked `gather(*[call(x) for x in million])` is an outage. You also still log usage per request; a batch is not one row unless the vendor's batch API says so.

Streaming many concurrent user chats is a different problem (backpressure). This note is about request-shaped work.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, overnight evals that run sequentially waste the clock and the laptop. Interviewers will ask how you run 1_000 classifications. They want chunks, a bound, per-item errors that do not cancel the group, and a usage row per item. They will ding a single try/except around the whole gather that drops 999 successes on one fail.

## How it works + one small example

Chunk the work. `for chunk in slices(items, 20): results += await gather(*[one(i) for i in chunk], return_exceptions=True)`. Map exceptions to a structured fail; keep successes. Persist usage as you go so a crash does not lose the ledger.

Example. 1_000 tickets. 20 in flight, 2s each, ~100s plus backoff. One poison ticket returns an exception; the other 19 in that chunk still save. You do not rerun the 999.

LangChain `abatch` is the same idea if you already have runnables — still wrap with a bound and per-item errors.

## Failure modes

1. **gather on the entire set.** Memory and 429s.

2. **return_exceptions=False.** One fail cancels the cohort.

3. **One usage row for the batch** of online calls. You cannot find the expensive item.

4. **Concurrent user writes** to the same order id.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see the chunk size, the per-item error path, and the usage write. A single gather over the whole set is a reject. Ask what happens to the 999 when one ticket poisons the batch.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Concurrency is for independent items; chunk them.
- Per-item errors must not cancel the cohort.
- Log usage per request, not once per gather.
- Timeouts stay per call.
- Framework batch helpers still need a bound.
- Do not concurrent-write the same resource.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. gather fails the whole group when one call 500s. What do you change? Capture per-item exceptions (return_exceptions or equivalent), record the fail, and keep the successes. Rerun only the failures. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you run 1_000 independent classifications without a stampede? Chunk them (for example 20 at a time), gather inside the chunk with per-item error capture, persist usage as you go, and apply a semaphore that matches the rate limit. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why not one usage row for a 20-call gather? You cannot find the expensive or truncated item, and finance cannot attribute cost. Each call still has tokens and a finish reason. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I run independent requests in bounded chunks, I keep per-item errors from sinking the group, and I log usage per request. A million-way gather is not a plan.

bounded-concurrency-rate-limits.explain:
## What it is

Vendors publish **rate limits** (RPM, TPM, concurrent requests). **Bounded concurrency** means you never have more in-flight calls than that budget (minus a safety margin). The primitive is a **semaphore** (or a queue with a worker count). Hope is not a bound. If you exceed the limit you get 429s, then retries, then a stampede — the opposite of throughput.

Bounds are per **key**, per **model**, and sometimes per **region**. A second feature that shares the key shares the budget. Global unlimited gather in one feature steals from another.

Jittered backoff on 429 is the partner of the bound. The bound reduces how often you 429; backoff saves you when you still do.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the first load test without a semaphore is a 429 festival. Interviewers will ask how you avoid being banned at 1_000 calls. They want: semaphore = min(safe_RPM, your_target), jittered backoff, a budget alarm. They will ding 'we retry 429' without a bound — that is how you DDoS the vendor with your own retries.

## How it works + one small example

`sem = Semaphore(8)` if the model allows ~12 concurrent and you share the key with another job. Each call: `async with sem: await complete(...)`. Measure 429 rate. If it is not ~0, lower the bound. If the vendor offers 100 concurrent and you need 10, do not set 100 'because we can'.

Example. Eval job and production chat share a key. Eval gets a semaphore of 4; chat keeps 8 reserved. A fairness split is a product decision. One unbounded eval will 429 the chat.

TPM (tokens per minute) can bind before RPM if your prompts are huge. Bound on the scarcer resource.

## Failure modes

1. **No bound.** Retries amplify the 429s.

2. **Bound of 1000** because the laptop has threads.

3. **Ignoring shared keys.** Staging eval knocks out production.

4. **Only RPM, ignoring TPM.** Huge prompts still 429.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for the semaphore value and which limit it came from. If there is none, reject. Ask how eval and chat share the key. Ask whether TPM was considered.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- A semaphore (or worker count) is the production bound.
- Set it from RPM/TPM/concurrent limits, minus a margin.
- Shared keys share a budget; reserve some for interactive traffic.
- Retries without a bound amplify 429s.
- TPM can bind before RPM on huge prompts.
- Hope is not a rate limit.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. An eval job and chat share a key; chat starts 429ing. What happened? The eval consumed the shared budget. Split semaphores, use a separate key, or run eval in the batch API. Do not let overnight jobs steal interactive quota. Then show the change you would ship the same week. You retry 429s with backoff but have no semaphore. Why is that unstable? Every caller still launches at once, all 429, all wait, all retry together (even with jitter, the herd is large). A bound reduces arrivals; backoff handles leftovers. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What primitive keeps you under a vendor rate limit? A semaphore or a fixed worker pool sized to the concurrent/RPM/TPM budget minus a margin. Retries alone do not keep you under; they can make it worse. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I bound in-flight calls to the provider's rate, minus a margin, with a semaphore. I split the budget across features that share a key, and I treat 429 retries without a bound as a stampede.

Shared keys share a budget; reserve some for interactive traffic.
Retries without a bound amplify 429s.

Hope is not a rate limit.

questions.a: From the vendor limit, minus a margin, minus what other features need on that key. Then lower it if 429 rate is not near zero.

async-and-batch-execution.explain:
## What it is

There are two different 'batch' ideas. **Online async**: your process fires concurrent live calls (previous notes) and waits seconds. **Batch APIs**: you upload a file of requests, the vendor runs them **offline** (minutes to hours), often cheaper, with no interactive SLA. LangChain `batch` is usually the first idea. OpenAI's Batch API is the second. Do not mix the words in a design review.

Use online concurrency for user-facing fan-out and for small evals you will watch. Use the batch API for overnight evals, backfills, and large classification dumps. Both still need schemas, validation, and usage rows. Batch needs idempotent inputs: the same file can be replayed.

Framework `abatch` does not give you the discounted batch API. You must call that API on purpose.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, running 50k evals online will 429 and cost more. Interviewers will ask how you run a big eval. They want: batch API if the vendor has one, else bounded online chunks; never a for-loop on a laptop overnight without a bound. They will also ask what you do not put on the batch API: anything a user is waiting on.

## How it works + one small example

Decision:

- User is blocked → online, timeout, small fan-out.
- 10k labelled tickets, results tomorrow → batch API, then a job that validates and writes.
- 200 evals you will iterate on this hour → bounded online.

Example. You submit `requests.jsonl` with request ids you minted. Hours later you download results keyed by those ids, validate, and store. A failed line does not rerun the file blindly; you resubmit the failed ids.

Pin the model snapshot on batch jobs. A night-long job that silently changes models is a bad experiment.

## Failure modes

1. **User-facing batch API.** They wait hours.

2. **Calling abatch and expecting a discount.** You still pay online.

3. **No request ids** in the file. You cannot join results.

4. **Rerunning the whole file** after a 2% fail.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which channel a job uses and why. If they say batch for a user turn, or abatch for a discount, correct them. Ask how failed lines are replayed.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Online async ≠ vendor batch API.
- Users stay on online calls with timeouts.
- Overnight evals and backfills belong on the batch API when it exists.
- Mint request ids so you can join results and retry fails.
- Framework batch is usually still online pricing.
- Pin the model snapshot on long jobs.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. 2% of a 50k batch file failed. What do you rerun? Only the failed request ids, after you fix the cause. Do not resubmit the whole file and double-write successes. Then show the change you would ship the same week. A PM wants the Batch API for the checkout chat. What do you say? No. Users cannot wait hours. Keep checkout online with a timeout. Use batch for evals and backfills. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is the difference between LangChain batch and a vendor Batch API? LangChain batch/abatch usually runs live concurrent calls at online prices. A vendor Batch API uploads a file, runs offline, and is often cheaper with no interactive SLA. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Online concurrency is for waits of seconds. The vendor batch API is for overnight, cheaper, no-SLA work. I do not put users on the batch path, and I do not call abatch a batch API.

the-throughput-cost-trade-off.explain:
## What it is

Concurrency, throughput, latency, rate limits, machine resources, and **cost** move together. More in-flight calls can raise throughput until you hit a limit; then you pay in 429s, retries (more tokens), longer p95, and sometimes a bigger machine. Tokens cost the same per call whether you run them sequentially or concurrently — except retries and failed duplicates, which concurrency can increase. Batch APIs trade latency for a cheaper token.

The trade-off is a **budget**: target throughput, p95 cap, 429 rate near zero, spend cap. You cannot maximise all four. Interactive traffic favours p95 and a reserved slice of the rate limit. Offline jobs favour throughput and cheaper channels.

Write the numbers. 'We made it faster' is not a trade-off.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, a load test that 'succeeds' at 50 rps with 8% 429s and 2× retries has not succeeded; it has doubled spend. Interviewers will ask what you give up when you raise concurrency. They want: possible p95, 429s, cost from retries, and other features on the key. They will ding a plan with no spend cap.

## How it works + one small example

Make a small table before you tune.

Example. Eval of 10k items. Sequential: 6 hours, $X, 0 429s. Concurrent 20: 25 minutes, $X, 0 429s. Concurrent 200: 20 minutes, $1.4X from retries, chat 429s. You pick 20 and a semaphore, or you move to the batch API for $0.5X and 4 hours.

Interactive: reserve concurrency, never let eval steal it. Alert on spend per hour and on 429 rate, not only on 5xx.

## Failure modes

1. **Maximising rps** with no 429 or spend budget.

2. **Ignoring retry tokens** in the cost model.

3. **One number** ('50 rps') without p95 or error rate.

4. **Overnight job on the interactive key** with no reservation.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for the four numbers. If they only have rps, the trade-off is missing. Ask what happens to retry spend at the proposed bound.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Concurrency trades throughput against p95, 429s, and retry cost.
- Parallel does not discount tokens; retries can inflate them.
- Write targets: rps, p95, 429 rate, spend.
- Reserve rate-limit for interactive traffic.
- Batch API is the usual cheaper, slower channel.
- A load test with 429s is a cost incident, not a win.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A load test hits 50 rps with 8% 429s. Is it a success? No. You are retrying, paying extra, and stealing budget. Lower the bound until 429s are near zero, then report rps and p95 together. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Does running 20 calls at once make each token cheaper? No. Price per token is the same online. You may finish wall-clock sooner. Retries can make the job more expensive. The batch API is the cheaper channel. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What do you give up when you raise in-flight LLM calls? Often tail latency, 429 headroom, and money if retries multiply. Throughput may rise until the scarcer limit. Interactive traffic on the same key can suffer. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat concurrency as a budget across throughput, p95, 429s, and spend. Tokens are not cheaper just because they run in parallel; retries can make them more expensive.

questions.a: Target throughput, p95 cap, 429 rate, and spend (or token) cap. Plus which key and model they apply to.

semaphore-as-the-production-primitive.explain:
## What it is

The **semaphore** (or a worker pool of size N) is the thing you actually ship. It is a counter: at most N calls are in flight; the N+1st waits. N is derived from the provider's concurrent/RPM/TPM limit, not from 'the machine felt fine'. Every online fan-out, every eval chunk, every retry path goes through the same primitive so you cannot accidentally open a second unlimited door.

A semaphore is not a queue with fairness unless you add one. It is not a circuit breaker (that opens on error rate). You often want all three: bound (semaphore), isolate (per-feature semaphore), and stop (breaker) when the vendor is sick.

Name it in the interview. 'We bound concurrency' without naming the primitive is fog.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the bug is the second entry point that forgot the semaphore: a new cron, a new script, a retry loop that launches calls outside the wrapper. Interviewers want the word semaphore (or worker pool) and the sentence that N comes from the vendor, not from hope. This is M2.8's production slogan.

## How it works + one small example

One wrapper: `async with rate_limit[model]: return await client.complete(...)`. All features import it. N lives in config next to the key. Example: `gpt-4o: 8`, `small-classifier: 20`. Changing N is a config change, not a hunt through gather()s.

Retries acquire the semaphore again; they do not sneak around it. Batch API jobs do not use this semaphore; they have their own submission cap.

Test: start N+5 calls, assert that in-flight never exceeds N (a counter you increment in the wrapper).

## Failure modes

1. **A gather that bypasses the wrapper.**

2. **N = 256** because that is the thread default.

3. **Retries outside the wrapper.**

4. **One global N** for a tiny model and a huge one that share nothing.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see the wrapper and the config N. Grep for raw client.complete outside it. If retries construct a new client, they probably skipped the bound.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Ship a semaphore (or pool); do not sprinkle gather().
- N comes from vendor limits, minus margin, per model/key.
- Retries acquire the same bound.
- A second entry point that skips the wrapper is an incident.
- Pair with a breaker when the vendor is sick.
- Test that in-flight never exceeds N.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A new cron calls the SDK directly and chat 429s. What was missing? The cron bypassed the wrapper. All entry points must acquire the same per-key semaphore (or use a separate key). Fix the door, not only the cron schedule. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Should retries skip the semaphore to 'catch up'? No. That is how you stampede. Retries wait their turn. If you are behind, lower arrivals or shed load. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is the production primitive for bounded LLM concurrency? A semaphore or fixed worker pool around the client wrapper, sized to the vendor limit. Every online call and retry acquires it. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The production primitive is a semaphore sized to the provider's rate, used by every online call including retries. Hope is not a bound.

Test that in-flight never exceeds N.

batch-apis-vs-online.explain:
## What it is

**Online** means the user (or your interactive job) is waiting: timeout in seconds, streaming optional, list price. **Batch APIs** are a different channel: submit, wait, download, often half price, minutes-to-hours latency, weaker SLAs. Overnight **evals** and backfills belong on batch. User-facing turns stay online. Mixing them is a product bug (users wait) or a cost bug (you paid list for 50k offline items).

Batch is not 'async' in the asyncio sense. Your process can be async online. Batch is an upload. Plan for eventual consistency: the result file arrives later; your job must be restartable and idempotent.

Not every vendor has a batch channel. If they do not, bounded online chunks are the fallback — still not a user path for 50k items.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, finance will ask why evals cost as much as production. The answer is usually 'we ran them online'. Interviewers will ask which channel you pick. They want this split in one breath: users online, overnight evals batch, timeouts versus files, list versus discount. This is the M2.8 interview sibling to the 1_000-calls question.

## How it works + one small example

Label each job in the repo: `channel=online|batch`. Example: nightly regression 8k items → batch, request ids, pin snapshot, validate on download. Lunch-time prompt tweak on 80 items → online bounded. Checkout chat → online, 20s timeout, reserved semaphore.

If batch is down, do not silently fail over 8k items to online without a spend alarm. That failover is a budget event.

## Failure modes

1. **Users on batch.** Support tickets about 'the button spun for an hour'.

2. **Evals on online** at list price by habit.

3. **Silent failover** from batch to online.

4. **Non-idempotent batch lines** so a replay doubles writes.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to label three jobs online vs batch. If evals are online at list price with no reason, push them. If a user path says batch, reject.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Online: seconds, users, list price. Batch: hours, files, often cheaper.
- Evals and backfills prefer batch; user turns never do.
- Label the channel in the repo.
- Failing batch over to online is a spend event.
- Batch lines must be idempotent and keyed by your request id.
- asyncio online is not a batch API.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Batch is down; a cron starts 8k online calls. What should happen? A spend/rate alarm and a conscious decision, not a silent failover. Prefer delaying the job. Dumping 8k onto the interactive key will 429 chat. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why must batch lines be idempotent? You will replay failed ids or the whole file. Without idempotency keys or upserts you double-write side effects. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Which jobs belong on a vendor Batch API? Overnight evals, backfills, and large offline classification — work that can wait hours and should pay less. Not user-facing turns. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Users stay online with a timeout. Overnight evals use the batch API when it exists. I label the channel on every job and I never silently fail a large batch over to list price.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: 1_000 calls without getting banned** is a spoken recipe: **concurrency cap** (semaphore sized to the limit), **jittered backoff** on 429/503, and a **budget alarm** (tokens or spend per hour, plus 429 rate). You add: chunk the work, per-item errors, separate keys or reserved quota for chat, and batch API if this is an eval. You do not say 'we retry a lot'.

This is M2.8's exam. They want the primitive and the restraint, not a thread count.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Every company that has a vendor key has been 429ed by its own eval. Interviewers use this question to see if you have. On the job it is also the design review for the first load test.

## How it works + one small example

Say, in order:

1. 'N-way semaphore from the vendor concurrent/RPM/TPM limit, minus a margin.'
2. 'Chunks of work, per-item errors, usage per request.'
3. 'Jittered backoff, cap on retries, no retry on 400/401.'
4. 'Alarm on 429 rate and spend; chat reserved if the key is shared.'
5. 'If it can wait until morning, Batch API instead.'

Close: 'Hope is not a rate limit.' If they ask about 1_000 user chats, you also mention backpressure and that you do not gather 1_000 streams unbounded.

## Failure modes

1. **Only retries**, no bound.

2. **N = 1_000** because the question said 1_000.

3. **No alarm.** You find out from finance.

4. **Forgetting the shared key** with production chat.


## How you would defend it in a review

Time the recipe. They must say semaphore, jitter, alarm. If they set N to 1000 or only mention retries, they fail the talking point.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Cap, jittered backoff, budget alarm — in that sentence.
- N comes from the limit, not from the item count.
- Reserve quota for interactive traffic.
- Prefer Batch API when the work can wait.
- Per-item errors and per-request usage.
- Retries without a bound are a stampede.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You remembered retries but not a bound. What happens at t=0? All 1000 launch, most 429, retries amplify, chat on the same key dies. The bound had to exist before the first retry. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why is N=1000 the wrong semaphore for 1000 items? The vendor will not allow 1000 concurrent. N is a rate-limit number (8, 20, 40), not the dataset size. The dataset is chunked over time. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Walk 1_000 LLM calls without getting banned. Semaphore sized to the vendor limit minus margin, chunked gather with per-item errors, jittered backoff on 429/503, alarms on 429 rate and spend, reserved quota for chat, Batch API if it can wait. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

One thousand calls: a semaphore from the vendor limit, jittered backoff, a spend and 429 alarm, and the batch channel if nobody is waiting. I do not set N to 1_000 because the question said 1_000.

common-api-failures.explain:
## What it is

LLM calls fail in boring, named ways. **401/403**: bad or expired key, wrong scope. **400**: your request is illegal (schema, context length, role sequence). **429**: rate limit. **5xx / 503**: vendor sick. **Network / timeout**: you never got a body. **Context-limit**: prompt too large (sometimes a 400 with a specific message). **Malformed output**: HTTP 200 but JSON or a tool call you cannot parse. **Content filter / refusal**: 200 with a finish reason that is not `stop`.

You must recognise these as different species. They do not share a retry policy. Treating all of them as 'try again' is how you loop on a bad key or a too-long prompt until the budget dies.

Log the species, not only 'error=true'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, the first on-call week is this list. Interviewers will ask you to name failure modes and one action each. They want this inventory, then the next note's retry map. A candidate who says 'sometimes the API fails' has not operated a client.

## How it works + one small example

Write a table in the wrapper: status or exception → species → action. Example: 401 → fail fast, page secrets. 400 context → shrink history, do not retry the same body. 429 → backoff. 503 → backoff. Timeout → retry once if the request id says it is safe. 200 + bad JSON → repair/reject (M2.4), not transport retry.

Keep an example payload per species in the playbook so the next hire does not confuse a refusal with an empty bug.

## Failure modes

1. **One catch-all retry.** 401 becomes a 10-second hang.

2. **Ignoring 200-malformed.** Users see blank bubbles.

3. **Not reading the error body.** A 400 that said context_length looks like a mystery.

4. **No species in the log.** You cannot graph 429 vs 400.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to list species without looking. If they only say timeout and 500, the inventory is thin. Ask what they do on a 200 with empty content.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Inventory: 401, 400, 429, 5xx, timeout, context, malformed, refusal.
- Species do not share a retry policy.
- 200 can still be a failure (malformed or refused).
- Read the error body; log the species.
- Context-limit is a shrink problem, not a backoff problem.
- A catch-all retry hides a bad key.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A 400 says context_length_exceeded. Do you backoff? No. The same body will fail again. Shrink or summarise history, drop retrieval, or split the task. Backoff is for 429/503. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why is HTTP 200 not enough to call a turn successful? Finish reason may be length or refusal, or the body may be unparseable. Inspect the response object before you accept. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Name six LLM API failure species and one action each. 401 fail-fast and fix the key; 400 read the body and fix the request; 429 backoff; 503 backoff; timeout retry if safe; context-limit shrink history; malformed 200 repair or reject; refusal show a canned decline. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I name the failure: auth, bad request, rate limit, vendor 5xx, timeout, context limit, malformed output, or refusal. Each species has its own action. I do not retry them as one pile.
